I love this game, it's like Zelda on crack.  Everything moves so fast, the music is upbeat, you have to spam attack button so continuously that it hurts your forearms.

Unfortunately, I beat this on Easy mode because I was really busy this week, I'll replay it on a "real" difficulty (maybe not Nightmare, but at least hard) when I have more free time and am not as busy with IRL stuff. Still, I think I can give it a fair review. I don't have time to give my usual brief description of the setting (you can look that up) but in terms of gameplay, it's much like the team based style of Dana and Monstrum Nox: Combat revolves around switching characters, blocking and dodging at just the right times to activate "Flash Guards" and dodge buffs, and using character skills to unlock new areas. However, it is a little primitive comparatively, the graphics are nowhere near as nice (understandable because its old) and it plays a little less smoothly than Dana and Monstrum Nox. It's still very fun though. The character art is cute and appealing, and much like the other Ys games, the characters themselves are so lovable they almost felt like my friends too, which I kinda needed after a shitty couple of weeks. The music is pretty good, not as good as Dana's but respectable nonetheless. I only have a couple of serious problems with it: First, a lot of the warp points have limitations on them that are only lifted once you get an item partway through the game, which struck me as kinda pointless. Second, the PC port is kinda buggy, it's a good thing you can save whenever you want because the game crashed pretty constantly, sometimes cutscenes froze up and sometimes it just closed randomly. Also, a lot of the game revolves around manipulating the environment with switches, etc. and whenever you do so a short cutscene plays, which is kinda annoying cause they take so long, I wish it could have been handled 'in engine' so to speak instead of reloading the entire area when platforms changed position. Finally, just a quibble on my part I suppose, but I found the ending kind of underwhelming. But in any case, these are small quibbles and the bugs are easy enough to fix with quick internet searches, I'm glad I played this and I'll revisit it when I'm doing better IRL. Hell, even if things never get better for me, I'm happy to have gotten this off my bucket list.

Many people may have been introduced to the Ys series through the recently released Ys VIII, and for those that are interested in delving deeper, or the ones that want to find a good place to start, Ys Memories of Celceta is a game to consider.

You play as Adol, a young man driven by his need to see the world and experience adventures. The story itself is simple, yet effective. Here you will not find any intricate plot twists or world-altering story events. This is, like with most of the games in the series, another fun adventure led by Adol. You'll explore the ancient forest of Celceta, a place not yet mapped by anyone due to the many dangers hidden within. At the start of the game, Adol is shown coming out of the forest, confused and without memories of who he is or what he was doing that led to that moment. A short prologue happens and it all leads up to an expedition to map the forest of Celceta and retrace the steps that Adol took, in order to reclaim his identity and lost memories. Along the way he meets different companions and the plot unravels. 

As this game is one of the first modern takes on the formula that the series has established over the years, it has some of the smoothest yet simplistic combat gameplay that you can find in a JRPG. It feels great and looks satisfying to see yourself tear through countless of enemies. As for the enemies themselves, there are many kinds that are vulnerable to different attacks. To exploit this, you can switch on the fly to one of your three available party members and pierce, slice or bash your way through them, dealing more damage in the process. There are special attacks that can be utilised by spending the power points in your combat gauge which naturally fills up while you kill opponents, and lastly there's also a special gauge that can only be used once it's entirely filled, and it does take a while, but once you can it enables you to unleash a strong attack combo that will almost surely decimate your foes or deal heavy damage against bosses. Do remember to use the correct attack type with the opposing enemy though, otherwise it will show to be a lot less effective in the same way it works with normal attacks.

The music, oh god, the music. If you heard anything about the Ys series, you'll probably at least know of its reputation of having great soundtracks, and this is no exception. While you battle and explore your way through forest, you're accompanied by catchy guitar riffs and melodic synthesizers. It all works to fire you up and keep going. Falcom's audio department never really disappoints in this category. On the other hand, when it comes to voice acting there's not much of it to be heard, and when you do it's just a single line followed by lots of silent text and the occasional grunt or vocal expression following a sentence. It's standard fare for these kind of JRPGs, but still something that could be improved on.

In terms of graphical fidelity, it does what it needs to do, but not much else. Honestly, Ys and most other projects of Falcom never really benefit from state-of-the-art visuals, most likely due to the fact that it's a smaller sized company and thus lack the funds to accomplish such feats. Although they do show improvement with this as time goes on, it's a slow crawl and never gets up-to-par with the more big-budget titles. So if you're picky about outdated graphics, this is something to keep in mind when considering your purchase. Still, from my experience, the gameplay makes up for this drawback for the most part, and that's where Ys excels in.

In conclusion, if you're looking for a fast-paced JRPG with tight gameplay, an adventurous story with simple yet charming characters, be sure to give Ys: Memories of Celceta a try if you can.

Ys: Memories of Celceta was originally released on PS Vita after Ys Seven.  MoC is an evolution of the gameplay from Seven, continuing the party based combat with the rock-paper-scissors vulnerabilities, but a faster skill system with the first attack auto charging to provide additional SP instead of needing to manually hold down the attack button.  This smooths out the learning curve while allowing veterans to dive right in.

This time Adol doesn't fall off a boat, but wanders into the city with no memory.  Adol is told by a friend that he left to explore the Great Forest, and after a few local events, he's once again spurred into action to - you guessed it - explore the Great Forest.  The allies he meets along the way fulfill the varies JRPG roles, and each has their own playstyle to keep things fresh, although personally I mainly played as Adol unless I was learning skills.

As a Vita port, the game performs great.  No lag or graphics issues, no crashes, and runs beautifully.  The graphics are a little blocky since they are uprezzed from the Vita's 960x544 resolution, but its much better looking than Ys Seven's PSP port did.  This also looks better than that horrid Joyoland port from a few years ago, so big props to XSEED on how to properly port a title to PC. (yes, I'm looking at THAT GAME)

Ys: Memories of Celceta is an easy recommendation to make.  Great gameplay, enjoyable music and plenty of challenge make this the best Ys release on PC since Ys Seven! (yes, I did it again)

Ys: Memories of Celceta is an action RPG built around fast combat, broad exploration, and a narrative centered on reconstruction of lost memories. After Adol emerges from the Great Forest of Celceta with no recollection of his past journey, the game tasks players with mapping the region while uncovering the truth behind his memory loss. This framework creates a clear structure that combines personal mystery with world discovery.

The plot unfolds through Adol’s encounters with ancient civilizations, political tensions in nearby towns, and the growing threat linked to the forest’s hidden power. Memory fragments serve as narrative markers, revealing past events in small but meaningful increments. This device provides pacing and context without slowing exploration, ensuring that story progression aligns naturally with field traversal.

Combat uses the series’ trademark speed, supported by the party-based system introduced in Ys Seven. Each character represents a specific damage type—slash, strike, or pierce—which encourages switching during encounters to break enemy defenses efficiently. Character-specific skills and finishers add depth, allowing players to build effective combinations while maintaining constant momentum.

Exploration is central to the experience. The Great Forest is divided into varied biomes, including dense jungles, sunlit plains, wetlands, and ancient ruins. Mapping these areas is part of the core progression, granting rewards for thorough coverage. Shortcuts, hidden areas, and environmental hazards create a sense of discovery that ties directly to the theme of recovering what was lost.

Villages and settlements provide structure between expeditions. They offer crafting, equipment upgrades, and side quests that flesh out regional conflicts and character relationships. These tasks reinforce a sense of community and give context to how the forest’s mysteries affect surrounding populations. The steady expansion of services reflects Adol and his companions’ growing influence.

Boss encounters deliver the game’s most challenging moments. Each fight relies on timing, movement precision, and knowledge of character roles. Arena designs vary significantly, forcing players to adapt strategies rather than relying on repetitive patterns. Once mastered, these battles highlight the strengths of the party-switching system and the game’s responsive controls.

Ys: Memories of Celceta succeeds through its integration of exploration, rapid combat, and narrative built around memory and rediscovery. The mapping mechanic provides a unique identity, while the streamlined progression keeps the adventure focused and accessible. For players seeking a dynamic action RPG with strong pacing and an emphasis on uncovering a world piece by piece, it stands as a solid and distinctive entry in the series.

Memories of Celceta is the 8th Y's game starring Adol Cristin, everyone's favorite kindhearted and stoic red-headed hero! I've been a fan of Y's since the snes days and it always served as a nice alternative for people who preferred action rpgs (akin to Crystalis and Zelda) over Final Fantasy. Indeed, Y's has evolved and grown,starting off more as a solo-hero hack n slash spell casting item hunt then becoming more of a party member managing beat em up still placing a lot of emphasis on exploration, boss battles, crafting, and choosing the right character to face off against the right enemies. From Y's 7 onward I'd say the series is akin to Secret Of Mana on performance enhancing cybernetic upgrades! There are also simalarities to Torchlight though instead of being "nameless heroes" the story includes and focuses on each person who joins Adol's party, allowing us to get to know them as actual people with their own hopes,fears,family dramas,and aspirations.

Celceta starts with Adol having amnesia. He and his mercenary friend Duren (Who is suspiciously similar to Dogi but still a different guy) are tasked with re-entering the huge forest and mapping out any major finds at the request of a female general and her occupying military contingent. Offered "big bucks" neither Adol or Duren have objections though Adol is more in it to find his lost memories and Duren is more in it for the monetary rewards. (Hey, a man has to eat and put a roof over his head afterall!) Regardless feats of daring and wacky misadventures soon ensue!

Y's has intuitive easy controls from the get go but you can re-map buttons at your leisure! Having played Y's 7 on the psp, Celceta very much the same though it "looks" nicer with improved visuals. The vistas in this game are truly breathtaking, regardless if the graphic engine is still dated by today's standards. Colors and details still shine thru and areas are still fun to explore as you run around bashing monsters and collecting materials to either enhance your weapons and armor or trade them in for more gold. Those aforementioned monsters are either weak towards piercing,slashing,or blunt damage so certain characters specialize slaying certain beasts. Additionally every character has an important skill (Duren can pick locks for example) that help you along your journey. "Sacred artifacts" also aid in this task as with them you can dive deeper under water while swimming or even shrink in size to get thru smaller tunnels. 

Every town has a hero as well as a mystery to be solved. (With poor Adol usually getting blamed for the current unfortunate events) so you'll be recruiting promising allies whilst usually trying to clear Adol's good name! It's from these quests you usually fight the biggest bosses (and mid bosses) whilst also learning more about the other main characters in your group. Karna for example is the proud chieftan's daughter. Initially it seems like she chose to be a huntress and a fighter whereas her brother became a bard and artisan but there's more to it than that and the revelation of the truth later makes her question her own worth and abilities. Ozma is the last surviving member of his family whom were beast-tamers of the sacred spartas, water dwelling drakes his people mount when going fishing in the great river. Supposedly the currents of the river are so chaotic that the spartas are needed to navigate the risky waters and simple boats will not cut it. Regardless when fish begin dying because of crimson poison coming from upstream, Adol is initially blamed and Ozma akin to Karna has to confront uncomfortable events surrounding his past (In this case related to Ozma's dead parents and the spartas themselves.). This sort of plot progression is very formulaic but it gets the job done. It's the little details and good writing that prevent things from becoming dull even if the usual fantasy tropes tend to be ever present.

As with other Y's games there is also a hidden kabal of "evil" pulling the strings who have their own schemes and goals, sometimes involving huge mega-monsters and other times involving creating super soldiers  thru masks that enhance the strength of their wearers whilst they go under hypnotic mind control. Y'know, the usual demented melancholic malaise of  tormented genius. (Pinky to my lips) Can I put friggin laser beams on something already or not?! It's my turn to shine! Ahem,apologies! I got a little ahead of myself there!

X-seed's port of Celceta performs marvelously and you can adjust just about any aspect you can think of to your hearts content whilst having visual representations of what those alterations will look like. 

Do I have a bone to pick? Nothing major. Perhaps the soundtrack is just a tad less inspired. I noticed dungeons in Celceta will share the same theme music whereas in Y's Origins every area had its' own unique tune and overall that soundtrack seemed far superior. (Oath of Felghana has a remarkable soundtrack too.) Don't get me wrong, what music is here is very good but the "variety of songs" seems to have taken a hit and the boss compositions for the most part come off as a little weaker than Y's previous audio offerings. What voice acting is present matches the characters nicely but it's obvious Falcom doesn't have the ridiculous budget of square/enix so beyond introductions of new characters,spoken dialogue is sparse and spread out over long distances. Frankly this doesn't bother me at all but it might be a point of contention with certain other gamers.

Pros

+ Fun combat with various super moves and super duper whooper grooves!

+Fun exploration

+well made dungeons and other vistas are a joy to explore

+Nice and handy transportation system 

+Very likable characters each with their own skills and specialalties to bring to the party

+Save anywhere

+We get to know more about Adol himself as an actual person,including his childhood

+Easy to understand upgrade,crafting,and trading system

+ Boss fights are still a pleasure and well thought out. I especially enjoyed luring the giant lantern fish into spiked urchins to gradually damage it as I swam for my life whilst it tried devouring me!

+Exploiting enemy weaknesses by switching off to the right character who has just the right weapon for the job keeps Celceta a cut above a typical meandering hack n slash. Slaying enemies with combos or shared special moves will net you bigger rewards as well!

+I recommend this game ESPECIALLY to people who enjoy Zelda,Secret of mana, and even Torchlight

+X-seed did an amazing job with the pc port

Cons

-Soundtrack while amicable isn't quite as "rockin" this time around

-Voice acting is also amicable but very limited.

Overall

Y's may not be the most original J-rpg franchise out there or make you ponder the universe and our place in the grand scheme of things BUT every Y's game I've ever played was immensely enjoyable and had remarkably exquisite level design. Adol inhabits this world that seems real on account we've gotten to experience so much of it thru his various adventures. If you love action adventure rpgs and metroidvanias picking up Celceta is a no-brainer. For the asking price it truly is a treasure!

It has been just three months since Steam saw its last Ys release, one plagued with technical issues upon launch at the hands of NIS America. Fortunately, the port here for Memories of Celceta is handled by XSEED, who have done an excellent job porting the title over.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[b]Fast-paced gameplay.[/b] The Ys series continues to be my go-to recommendation for those that want a fun JRPG experience without the turn-based combat or relatively slow nature that dominates the genre. Memories of Celceta picks up the pace early on and does not stop from there, immediately throwing the player into a world full of colorful environments, likable characters, and cool boss fights. As for the enemies scattered throughout this world, there seemed to be no end to their diversity. Even towards the very end of the game I was still being presented with new enemies, each with their own unique design and move set. The story maintained this quick pace as well, with dialogue scenes that never really dragged out the experience. This pacing was kept up until the very end and left me feeling very satisfied with the experience.

[b]Fun combat.[/b] The skills and type-matchups make the combat immensely more interesting – something more than just a hack and slash fiesta. Certain characters do more damage depending on enemy types and certain skills even allow for different playstyles. For example, I made heavy use of a dashing attack on my main character, which, when combined with the ice stats on my weapon, made for some pretty strategic combat. I would dash into a group of enemies, freezing many of them in the process, get a few hits in before they thawed, then back out to avoid unnecessary damage. This of course is made possible through the game’s incredibly responsive dodging. All it takes is one tap of the dodge button and my character goes rolling in whatever direction I choose. In fact, I traveled the game world by constantly dodge rolling because it was just that fast. All of these elements combined make for some pretty fun combat.

[b]Great soundtrack.[/b] Yet again I am here playing another Ys game with another stellar soundtrack. The soundtrack for Memories of Celceta is full of all of the traditional JRPG tracks one would expect, but done so in a masterful way by Falcom Sound Team jdk. There are lively town themes, ominous dungeon tracks, and, of course, action-packed battle themes. The soundtrack may not be the best in the series, but Falcom Sound Team jdk has yet to produce a disappointment and the soundtrack here is no exception. My favorite track ended up being To the Stage of a New Era.

[b]Well-done port.[/b] The last Ys game to release on Steam, Ys VIII, had a number of technical issues upon launch at the hands of publisher NIS America. Fortunately, XSEED has done quite the opposite here with Memories of Celceta. The game runs super-smooth at 1080p 60fps and, despite the fact that I played through the entire game before launch, I only ran into a single technical issue (which I will discuss later). On top of that, the porting team went above and beyond with the game’s settings menu. It comes in the form of a launcher that explains what each and every setting does and even includes pictures that note the differences between each setting. That same launcher also allows the game’s auto-save feature to be configured, a feature that is completely independent from the saves featured in-game, as a sort of emergency backup system. This is a godsend for JRPGs, as losing progress due to a power outage is one of the worst feelings ever. And speaking of godsends, the launcher also has an option to toggle the game’s startup logos, allowing players to jump right back into the game without having to view the five or so splashes beforehand. The port is just really well-done overall and I only hope that more ports follow the example set here by XSEED.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[b]Wonky camera.[/b] The camera for Memories of Celceta can be a bit troublesome at times. The only control the player has over it is a basic zoom in and out function, the rest being handled by the game. Normally, the game is pretty good at figuring out the right camera angle, but there were several points during my playthrough that had me wishing for a completely player-controlled camera, especially during the swimming segments. The camera at least does a bare minimum job, but it would be so much better if it could be configured further.

[b]Some game freezes.[/b] The only technical issue I ran into during my playthrough would be that of some minor game freezes. The first time I ran into this issue I had feared a game crash, but fortunately it turned out to just be a series of short freezes. When these freezes occurred, the game would lock itself up for a second or two, then resume, then freeze for another second or so, then resume and repeat the process a couple more times. Although this issue only happened to me maybe six or seven times, it is still a technical issue nonetheless.

[h1]Overall:[/h1]
On top of the fun and fast-paced gameplay already present in the original game, the port here is very well-done, including a variety of options to really make the game shine on PC. Even so, the camera can be a bit troublesome at times and the port is not “perfect”, but it is definitely enough to warrant a recommendation, even for those that have never played an Ys game before.

[code]Despite being a little rough around the edges with a few odd gameplay decisions and a weak story, Ys IV: Memories of Celceta remains a fun 15-20+h action-RPG that – due to its self-contained plot – should be enjoyable for franchise newcomers as well[/code]

Before moving on to talk about the actual game itself, let’s quickly go over where to place [i]Memories of Celceta[/i] in the [i]Ys[/i] franchise, as this might be a bit confusing. [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] takes place between the events of [i]Ys II[/i] and [i]Ys III: The Oath in Felghana[/i], which makes it the fourth entry in the franchise to play if you’re following the “story order” suggested by [url=https://www.digitalemelas.com/index_ys.php]DigitalEmelas[/url]. That said, the story of [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] is self-contained to the point where even newcomers to the franchise shouldn’t have any trouble following the story, since protagonist Adol has not only travelled to a new land but also lost all of his memories as well.

While this explains where to put [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] in terms of story, there’s more to be said about what kind of game [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] actually is – but feel free to skip this next paragraph if you’re not interested in more details of the game’s history.

This Steam version, which released in 2018, is a graphically enhanced (but offering no new content) port of the 2012 PS Vita game of the same name. Said Vita game, which was developed by Nihon Falcom, is actually a remake of 1993’s [i]Ys: Mask of the Sun[/i] (developed by Tonkin House) and [i]Ys: The Dawn of Ys[/i] (developed by Hudson Soft). This might sound confusing at first, but the explanation is [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ys_(series)] actually quite simple:[/url] From 1987 - 1989, the first three [i]Ys[/i] games were developed and published by Nihon Falcom. However, after completing [i]Ys III[/i] in 1989, the creators of the series (Masaya Hashimoto and Tomoyoshi Miyazaki) left Nihon Falcom and went on to establish their own studio (“Quintet”, responsible for [i]Act Raiser[/i] or [i]Terranigma[/i]). As a result, Nihon Falcom outsourced the development of what should be the new [i]Ys IV[/i] to two other studios, who had handled various port of the previous [i]Ys[/i] games: Tonkin House, now responsible for the Super Famicom version of [i]Ys IV[/i], and Hudson Soft, tasked with developing the PC version instead. While the two resulting games might share the same setting, basic plot and characters, they actually differ in terms of enemies, levels, story delivery and more. Afterwards, it was Tonin House’s [i]Ys IV: Mask of the Sun[/i] that went on to be considered the “canon” version of [i]Ys IV[/i] for a few years – at least, until Nihon Falcom themselves decided to create a now-canon version of [i]Ys IV[/i] with the 2012 PS Vita remake we’re seeing ported here: [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i].

As a remake, [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] does not make use of the “Bump System” present in [i]Ys I & II[/i] (or the original [i]Ys IV[/i] games) but went with a tag-team party system similar to the one from [i]Ys Seven[/i] instead. Up to three chosen characters from your party are fighting at the same time, two of which are controlled by AI – pressing a button switches the character the player is currently controlling. Apart from evading and guarding, normal attacks build up “SP”, which in turn can be spend on unleashing select skills – unleash enough, and you’ve filled your “EXTRA” gauge, which allows for one especially powerful attack. Basically, [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] is about switching to the right character for each enemy (the right attack types equals more damage dealt), evading/guarding against enemy attacks and performing combos through attacks and skills in real time. It’s not an especially deep combat system, just spamming attacks/skills should work well enough on lower difficulties, but it’s fast, responsive and flashy enough for a good time regardless.

Coupled with this satisfying real-time combat is exploring the Forest of Celceta, the main “gimmick” of [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i]. Exploring the semi open-world map isn’t only demanded by the story and necessary to reach the next quest objective, but mapping the areas beyond that also rewards you with additional items, Adol’s memories and materials used to create/refine various equipment. Furthermore, a NPC gives you additional rewards based on your map completion percentage, which really drives home just how much [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] wants to be a game that’s all about adventurous exploring and fighting through uncharted territory – complete with the occasional dungeon featuring small puzzles and boss fights as a highlight, of course. Typical for a Nihon Falcom game, [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] also features an exceptional soundtrack, with more than just a few [url=https://youtu.be/UH533aWi9Rs?si=tEJdcsGZrs5_Ze2L]fantastic tracks[/url] that immediately get stuck in your head.

But while the combat is fun, the music fantastic and the exploring usually rewarding enough to be worth the occasional detour, [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] unfortunately isn’t without its faults as well. The story, while usually not the strong suit of the [i]Ys[/i] games to begin with, is largely predictable, quite cliched and frankly overall uninteresting. The characters, including the party members, are mostly shallow and the story just stops abruptly once the credits start rolling, rather than actually ending and giving closure to the various characters.

In terms of gameplay, there’s the unnecessarily unfriendly fast-travel system that only starts to actually become useful halfway through the game for some reason. Similarly, the ability to sprint is granted far too late in my opinion, especially since the (mostly uninteresting) side-quests do require a bit of backtracking at times. But even sprinting and fast travelling doesn’t help with the map completion at the end of the game – achieving 100% can be quite painful since the game doesn’t do a great job of showing you what smaller areas you’ve missed exactly. Additionally, some maps require the player to “hug” every border and crevice in order to “uncover” some of the far-away map borders necessary for 100% completion – an annoying decision.

Lastly, while it’s great to have characters with multiple abilities – Adol can collect his memories, Duren can open locked chests and so one – switching to the right character can be unnecessarily time-consuming during the late-game dungeons that require abilities from all party members. The same goes for artifacts required for puzzles, which can only be switched by going through multiple menus as well. Speaking of menus, it's also fair to say that [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] isn’t the best-looking game out there – its Vita origins are quite clear, from puzzles that obviously used to require a touchscreen to the small-sized maps, an overall low-detailed world with few enemy types and characters as well as the general UI structure.

Still, overall [i]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/i] remains a fun 15-20+h action-RPG that doesn’t overstay its welcome unless you’re going for all achievements. Satisfying combat, fun exploration and a great soundtrack make this game a good choice for action-RPG fans, even if it might not reach the heights of other games in the [i]Ys[/i] series. Since the plot is mostly self-contained, newcomers to the franchise shouldn’t be afraid to try this game as well, although there are admittedly even better and more popular games in the [i]Ys[/i] series to start out with.

Falcom took it in their hands to finally remake this numbered Ys game, creating the definitive one to play if you're playing through it. For those that don't know, prior to this game, there was: The Mask of the Sun and Dawn of Ys. It wasn't until Memories of Celceta that Falcom put their foot down on what version would be the one people would go for. And, for what it's worth, this title holds up quite nicely in the series as a whole.

Graphically, the game can be a bit of a mix bag. I find the visuals overall to be fine, with some brief moments that are pretty nice. This might be due to the fact that the game was originally on the Playstation Vita, making some consolations when porting to PS4 and Steam. However, while the visuals might not be the greatest, the soundtrack is everything you could ask for in the series. Absolutely amazing throughout every environment and helps pull things together in your journey.

Gameplay is a formula Ys has been using for a few games, but it is still quite nice. The game doesn't overwhelm you with mechanics and, the ones they do offer, isn't mandatory if you just want to just experience the game. With that said, on hard or higher difficulty, I can see wanting to familiarize yourself with what the game does offer.

The writing can be a bit up-and-down. I would say that most of it, outside of the main story, is pretty nice. While some of it might not lead anywhere, it does help to make the people you encounter a bit more alive. The party members, I find, are typically either focused on for their personality and character depth, or just for their place in the story; the latter tagging along after their moment in the story is resolved because they're a party member and they have to.
With the main story as a whole feeling like a snowball which become out-of-control. Adol, in an early adventure, loses his memory and is trying to piece things back together. His new partner, Duren, convincing him to help fill a map in of the surrounding area, giving Adol an excuse to go back out there and try to figure out what has happened. [spoiler]This doesn't really change and you find a couple of areas where you have to fix a misunderstanding between you and the people living there while also resolving the issue at hand. However, about 60% through, or even a bit more, the story suddenly ramps up considerably. It wouldn't be all-too-jarring, but the pacing at which things move at leaves a bit to be desired.[/spoiler]

With all that said, I did love my time with this game. I might be biased, but there is something about journeying with Adol that will always put a smile on my face. In addition, the game is ~$25, and less on sale, which is a steal for a nearly 20-hour experience.

Ys: Memories of Celceta is not my favourite Ys experience. I do have issues with the product overall, and would recommend a few others I've played over it. However, there is still love and passion put into the title. The gameplay is enjoyable, the music brings you right there into the world. And traveling with Adol on just another one of his journeys is just as enjoyable as it always has been.

Ys: Memories of Celceta is an action/rpg/adventure game, with a great cast of characters, amazing music, interesting story and addictive gameplay.
This game is a part of a whole franchise, that started in 1987. It was originally a PS Vita game, but XSeed ported it to PC and polished it even further. 

[h1] The Story[/h1]
Our protagonist arrives in the town of Casnan without any memories about himself. After collapsing from fatique he meets an information dealer - Duren, who claims that he know our hero and his name is "Adol Christin". The last time Duren heard anything from Adol is when he went to explore the Great Forest of Celceta. It seems like a dangerous place and no one ever made it back alive, aside from Adol. God knows what happened to Adol while he was there, but this amnesia is a result of that. After some (tutorial) events Duren joins the party and it's the time to collect Adol's memories and explore the Great Forest again.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1470681325

[h1] The Gameplay[/h1]
Ys is fast-paced action-rpg, featuring realtime combat. You can utilize normal attacks, skills and finishing moves to finish off your targets. Try to use your ultimate moves(default keyboard button "5") to finish off bosses for extra bonus. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1481516067
You can also dash and block, and doing so with perfect timing will grant you bonus effects, for example, if you do a perfect dash-dodge, you'l get a significant movespeed boost.

Aside from battle aspects, there's a lot of weapons and armor, upgrade system and crafting.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1481513082
The game also offer a lot of sidequests and even some "hidden" quests, which will not appear in your quest log/journal. It's pretty much impossible to find everything on your first playthrough, so if you're short on time, use this guide https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/vita/643152-ys-memories-of-celceta/faqs/68364 and don't miss anything. But it may be hard to avoid spoilers, so it's up to you.

[h1] The Final Verdict[/h1]
8/10
Ys: Memories of Celceta is a perfect choice if you want to play a great action-rpg and it's fine to start with this game if you are new to this series. You will be surprised how good story is and by well developed characters. If you like this game, you can check other games from Falcom, like Trails of Cold Steel.


Bonus: this is the current timeline for the events of the series.

1. Ys Origin - prequel, takes place about 700 years before Ys I
2. Ys I & II - The start of the series
3. Ys: Memories of Celceta - the game takes place a year after the events of Ys II, and about a year before Ys: The Oath in Felghana
4. Ys: The Oath in Felghana
5. Ys V (this one is not available atm)
6. Ys VIII: Lacrimosa of Dana
7. Ys VI: The Ark of Napishtim
8. Ys Seven - takes place about 6 months after Ys VI

This list will help you if you want to dig deeper into Adol's journal and his adventures.
And to answer the question - yes, it's perfectly fine to start with this game if you're not familiar with Ys series.

[h1] Story and Setting [/h1]

The story revolves around the adventurer Adol Christin. For generations, the Christin family has been known for exploring the world, therefore it is also quite clear that Adol wants to travel the world and see every corner. One day, he sets out to explore the Forest of Celceta, being lured by the fact that no traveler has ever returned from it.

The story takes place one year after the events in [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/223810/Ys_I__II_Chronicles/]Ys II[/url] and when Adol regains consciousness, he remembers nothing. Only when the mysterious traveler Duren enlightens him that Adol was the first to get out of the forest in one piece, could he remember a few fragments.

The local ruler, Griselda, heard about this event and summoned the young adventurer to her place. When Adol was with Griselda, she made him an incredible offer: he should map and explore the entire world of Celceta. Overwhelmed by this statement, he agreed. With Duren in tow, the duo set out to explore the world. They will discover many dangers, new friends, and the indomitable wilderness. But the real evil is already waiting for them.

Heroes without memories are a rather overused role-playing game cliché in my book, but on one hand, the narrative template dates back to the early 1990s. The flashback puzzle, some of which can even be actively played, is still interesting dramaturgically: you are confronted with deeds you can't remember, meet people you seem to have disappointed. Only when the last gaps in the memory journal close - a handy log of your adventures, which can be viewed at any time -  do you become aware of all the tragic connections that the forest has devoured.

[h1] Exploration [/h1]

The already mentioned story aspect may sound like an open world, but that is deceptive. In typical JRPG fashion, you are given a mission objective and work through it. Meanwhile, there is a lot to see. Again and again, you'll be confronted by different monster sprites, huge waterfalls, or special sights.

With a simple click on the option key, you can open the map, which turns out to be enormously important. Here you can observe how with each newly explored place, the entire map is slowly revealed. This is not only visually recognizable, but also in terms of percentages.

[h1] Gathering and Crafting [/h1]

Besides uncovering the map, you can find quite a lot in this game. Grasses or flowers want to be harvested and woods and stones need to be mined. If you move through the world with Adol, he can pull out his sword at any time and use it. If he does this now with said objects, the raw materials of it fall off. Since there are many sources of raw materials at every corner of Celceta, you collect an enormous amount of items in the course of your playthrough.

The found items can be exchanged in every city. Be it at the local blacksmith, who makes new weapons from skins and ores, or at the merchant, who gives you money in contrast. Besides crafting weapons, you can also buy them. Once you've equipped Adol with the latest arsenal of weapons, the third option is to improve and refine them with the resources you've collected. The last way to sell your collected resources is to trade them. In this way, you can obtain/exchange high-quality material for many low-quality materials. The amount of items offered in this entry is definitely justified and important to survive in this world.

[h1] Combat [/h1]

When you travel through the Forest of Celceta, you are not on your own. Besides the informant Duren, a total of four other characters join Adol to help him. The battles run in real-time and are extremely smooth thanks to the unlimited framerate.

Each character has an arsenal of abilities at their disposal, and up to four actions can be taken and used in battle. Therefore, you can freely decide which ability you want to take with you since you get more and more over the course of your playthrough. However, to be really effective in the fight against the fauna in Celceta, the basic attack type must be chosen optimally. Either the hero can punch, stab or cut using his individual weapons. These work on the rock-paper-scissors principle. If you inflict damage on an enemy, and it glows yellow, you know that the attack is very effective. If, on the other hand, you see blue color, you should change your character as soon as possible. The aforementioned change also works very easily because you can switch back and forth between the characters with a single button press. The freedom of movement offered in the fights has been implemented very well. Fast sprints and evasive maneuvers can also be realized without any hassle. The fights are never unfair, and you have a satisfying feeling after defeating the spectacular bosses because each boss also has its own mechanic which you have to overcome.

The camera is unfortunately a negative point that I have to address because you can't move it. It is always fixed on one point and often leads to situations where you can’t see enemies or get attacked out of nowhere. I do not understand why this was not implemented.

[h1] Fragments [/h1]

In order to cure Adol's amnesia, small glowing orbs can be found all over the world. These symbolize the lost memories of the young adventurer and tell a small part of his story. Besides deepening the bond with the main character, you also get a permanent status boost, hence why you're eager to find the memory scraps throughout the game.

[h1] Technical [/h1]

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

The game captivated me much more than the first two entries. This is due to the fact that the story remains in the background until the end, small story snippets loosen up the game, but never interrupt the gameplay in a disturbing way. This creates a great flow of discovery and entertaining battles. Unreserved recommendation for all friends of action role-playing games from Japan, who can overlook the somewhat outdated technology and graphics. However, the story and gameplay are still appealing today. You direct a steadily growing group of heroes through the secrets and dangers of a forest that holds the key to your own past. With the use of individual talents and skills, you not only clear all kinds of obstacles, but also enemies out of the way, while you diligently collect loot, and work it into your equipment to keep the upper hand in dynamic real-time battles. Fans of old-school RPGs shouldn't be put off by the unimpressive exterior.

Ys: Memories of Celceta, developed by Nihon Falcom and published by XSEED Games and Marvelous USA, Inc., is an exhilarating action role-playing experience that blends fast-paced combat, rich exploration, and a deeply personal narrative centered on discovery and memory. It represents one of the more experimental entries in the long-running Ys franchise, revisiting the world of Ys IV with a modernized structure and Falcom’s signature flair for momentum and adventure. The story begins with series protagonist Adol Christin staggering into the frontier town of Casnan, stripped of his memories and without any recollection of the journey that brought him there. Before long, he teams up with a roguish information dealer named Duren and is tasked with charting the mysterious and uncharted Forest of Celceta—a vast, living labyrinth that holds secrets not only of the land itself but of Adol’s forgotten past. This setup immediately positions the game as a fusion of personal and geographical exploration, with memory, identity, and discovery serving as its unifying themes.

The mapping system is at the heart of Memories of Celceta’s design, and it’s what makes the game feel so distinctive. Rather than revealing the entire world from the outset, the game encourages you to uncover it piece by piece, creating your own detailed map as you traverse the wilderness. Every new area you explore gradually fills in your chart, rewarding curiosity and persistence with tangible progress. The mechanic transforms exploration into something tactile and satisfying—each step into unknown territory feels like genuine discovery. The forest itself is vast and diverse, ranging from dense woodlands and sunlit ruins to subterranean caverns and ancient temples. As your map expands, so too does your sense of achievement, and returning to previously visited areas with new tools or abilities often reveals shortcuts, hidden treasures, or previously inaccessible regions. The cartographic structure lends a natural rhythm to the gameplay, constantly giving you small goals that feed into a greater sense of adventure and mastery.

Combat is where Falcom’s expertise shines most brightly. Like other modern Ys titles, Memories of Celceta employs real-time, party-based action that feels fluid and immediate. You control one character at a time while two AI companions fight alongside you, and you can switch between them at will to exploit enemy weaknesses. Enemies are categorized by the types of damage they are susceptible to—slash, strike, or pierce—so quick tactical switching becomes a key part of success. The system is fast and responsive, emphasizing timing and rhythm over sheer statistics. Skills can be mapped to buttons for instant execution, and defensive mechanics like the Flash Guard and Flash Move reward perfect timing with temporary invulnerability or slowed enemy movement. These flourishes make combat both accessible and skill-based, rewarding precision without ever feeling punishing. Boss battles, in particular, are a highlight: each encounter tests reflexes and pattern recognition in ways that keep fights tense and satisfying. Even after dozens of hours, the flow of battle remains gratifyingly kinetic, with smooth animations and impactful sound design reinforcing the game’s sense of urgency.

Narratively, Memories of Celceta follows Adol’s search for his lost memories as he pieces together fragments of his past scattered throughout the land. Each recovered memory expands not only his personal story but also the broader history of Celceta itself, revealing the hidden truths behind its civilizations, the enigmatic mask at the center of the plot, and the ancient powers that shaped the world. The amnesia trope is a familiar one, but Falcom uses it effectively as a device to tie exploration and storytelling together. Adol’s lost identity mirrors the player’s gradual understanding of the land—both hero and player rediscover the world simultaneously. Alongside him, a cast of companions with distinct personalities and fighting styles join the adventure, adding warmth and humor to the journey. While the writing can be straightforward and the characters sometimes archetypal, their camaraderie and emotional sincerity give the narrative weight. The pacing of the story allows moments of reflection between bursts of action, and though it never aims for deep philosophical complexity, it maintains a consistent tone of optimism and determination that fits the adventurous spirit of the series.

Visually, the game bears traces of its PlayStation Vita origins, but Falcom’s art direction ensures that it remains appealing on modern hardware. The environments are vibrant and richly colored, capturing the lushness of the forests and the ancient majesty of the ruins you uncover. On PC, the game benefits from smoother frame rates, sharper textures, and improved lighting, making traversal and combat feel crisp and fluid. The interface is clean and functional, maintaining a clear focus on accessibility. Character models and environmental detail are modest compared to contemporary RPGs, but the art style’s consistency and the game’s colorful world design more than compensate for its technical limitations. The soundtrack, composed by Falcom’s legendary in-house team, the JDK Band, elevates every moment with a blend of energetic rock, orchestral anthems, and serene ambient pieces. From pounding battle themes to wistful exploration tracks, the music enhances the game’s momentum and reinforces its emotional beats, often propelling the player forward through sheer enthusiasm alone.

In terms of structure, Memories of Celceta strikes a balance between focused progression and open-ended exploration. The main story unfolds across a clear trajectory, but the player is encouraged to stray off the beaten path to complete side quests, gather resources, and uncover secrets hidden across the map. Towns and settlements act as rest points and quest hubs, providing context and variety between stretches of wilderness. There’s also a crafting and upgrading system that lets you refine weapons and armor, adding new properties or enhancing stats, giving players a constant sense of growth. The overall pacing remains strong throughout, though the final third introduces some backtracking and repetition that can slightly undercut the sense of forward momentum. Still, the satisfaction of completing the map, mastering new skills, and uncovering the mysteries of Celceta keeps the experience compelling from start to finish.

Ultimately, Ys: Memories of Celceta is a confident and exhilarating adventure that embodies everything fans have come to love about Falcom’s design philosophy—tight gameplay loops, expressive music, and a world that rewards exploration. It may not reach the visual sophistication of newer entries like Ys VIII or IX, but its spirit of discovery and fast, fluid combat hold up remarkably well. The combination of strong mechanics, memorable world-building, and the sense of progression tied to mapping and memory make it one of the more satisfying action RPGs in Falcom’s extensive catalog. For veterans of the series, it offers a chance to see Adol’s legend from a new angle; for newcomers, it serves as a welcoming entry point that captures the heart of what makes the Ys franchise endure. It’s not just a journey through an untamed forest—it’s a journey through the act of adventure itself, a reminder that discovery, no matter how many times it’s retold, never truly loses its wonder.

Ys is a series of Action JRPGS from Nihon Falcom and Memories of Celceta is a great part of it. Celceta is technically a remake of the fourth game Mask of the Sun but chronologically occurs before Oath in Felghana which is a remake of the third Ys game (a little confusing) 

Story
Ys games are not traditionally story heavy (at least not as much as the Kiseki series) though more recent games have skewed that way (Ys VIII being the prime example) Celceta I would say is somewhere in between it isn’t as short as the earlier games but it doesn’t take overly long to beat just the main story.

You play as Adol the Red on his journey through the forest of Celceta to recover his lost memories (it's not because of a shipwreck) throughout his adventure you will meet with a variety of characters each with their own little backstories and reasons for joining Adol on his Adventure, as a heads up I found the ending to be a little disappointing as it just kinda cuts off but it didn’t sour my overall opinion of the game.

Gameplay
Celceta uses the party based system that first appeared in Seven, this means quick combat where you will be expected to switch up characters to deal effective damage against different types of enemies. Your main options for avoiding damage are Flash Guard and Flash Move, which involve timing a button press to guard and timing a button press to dodge respectively the timing of these isn’t too hard to get down and you can always practice on normal enemies to prepare you for boss fights.

With that being said I didn’t find the game to be particularly difficult on the NORMAL difficulty setting (In contrast to Oath in Felghana) so I would recommend upping the difficulty to either HARD or NIGHTMARE if you want a bit more challenge.

Sound
Ys games always have great soundtracks and Celceta is no different, I do wish there were a few more tracks but considering the length of the game the music doesn’t get old. The game now has both English and Japanese voicing options. I left the game on English as I found the voice acting to be pretty good. There are also some recognisable voices for Kiseki fans as well.

Port 
I didn’t run into any issues playing this game on Windows 10, I recommend unchecking Display Launcher on Startup in the Configuration Tool and also Disabling HDR, I don’t have a HDR monitor but I don’t believe that this is true HDR as all it seems to do is blow out light sources I found the game looked more appealing with the setting off and it also greatly improved my frame rates from 80 - 90ish to 144fps.

I also tested the game on Linux (Pop_OS 20.04) and only ran into one issue, the cutscenes do not play. Luckily this only affects the very start and the very end of the game and you can find the cutscenes in the movie folder of the games files and play them manually.

I played the game a lot on the Vita, sadly not being able to finish it before I gave up on that sinking ship of a platform (thanks Sony) I've only played a a few hours at this time of writing the review here but so far it's a pretty straight forward port- in ways. 

Let me explain, the game's got some good options to tweak graphics and even has an unlocked 120fps+ option which is nice to see. Lets you even customize the buttons you're getting prompted with, 360/PS3/etc which is fairly rare, so they certainly put in the effort to say the least in that regard. 

Where it's a straight forward port is kinda where I'm not sure I'm super happy with. The interface is gigantic on the screen, none of the scaling is altered and it's all pretty low-res since it was on the Vita- so things are both large for the small screen AND for touch controls (I haven't tested if touch works in this). So everything feels kinda huge on screen and the camera is very zoomed in- in some spots. Camera control is also very limited, you can zoom in and out like the vita version. There is no adjusting how the camera is angled. So if you don't like what you see in screenshots? Well you can't change that so, take that how you will. 

The game itself has aged and show's that it's not very refined, this shows a lot in the opening cutscene where walk cycles don't match up with how the characters move, animation in these scenes is very simplistic but get the job done. 

Okay, so there's a lot of negative there, is this worth your money? I would say yes. The presentation of the story is a bit wonky but it gets the job done. The combat is fast and starts off simple but opens up a lot more as you progress. Playing on Hard Mode is where you're gonna get more tension and fun out of the gameplay since it will force you to not rely on taking hits but instead flash guard/dodging (guarding/rolling at the last minute to slow-mo the enemies so you can omni-slash the crap out of them) and your characters unique skills. 

Each character has their own perks, sword, blunt, spear, daggers all play into the enemies weaknesses that'll stun/kill them faster- all of this is passive, just need to let the character do their thing or switch to them yourself. Characters all have their own skill that you activate that take from a shared MP pool you refill by attacking- letting your character wait a second will net you a larger sum of MP restored.  So, combats fun, frantic and deep enough that it's not just a button masher. Characters with you are also active in combat, you can set them to passive if you fear they're going to get their face smashed but that's not TOO much a worry since the game gives some leeway, they can't seem to be taken down past 1HP, so if you get hit with a big AOE, your allies might survive with 1HP because of this, letting you run for safety. 

You also gather stuff for buffing weapons while you're out, your characters will thankfully both point out these gathering spots AND they will harvest it themselves. 

It's a fun game, the story isn't going to win any awards as it's fairly simple, predictable and straight forward. You a warrior with amnesia is trying to figure out how you lost your memory as you explore the place you lost it. A twist mid way through lets you know how it happened and there's more twists to be had. I called most of them and this was my first Ys game so it's not so much a surprise. 

Also, apparently this is a remake of a remake. It was a SNES game, then remade on  PS2 then remade for Vita and now ported years later to PC. WEIRD, but all fairly different apparently. 

Either way, if this is your first Ys game you're not missing much from what I understand. It's the same character, but just a different adventure and I don't think there's any references to previous ones. I only saw ONE reference in Ys VIII to this game and that's about it. What you need to know: Adol is an adventurer who winds up in a sticky spot and has to adventure his way out. Sometimes his friend Dogi is there to do stuff. 

Also because I didn't have a good point to mention it, the music in this game is really, really good. Fits the fast paced adventure, all tunes are pretty great. I had to mention this because it's apparently a sin to not mention the great tracks in these games. I guess since the series has been fairly obscure for decades the fans gotta have something to cling to, which makes sense. It's been around since the ...Turbo Grafix 16/PC Engine and stayed obscure till this game/Ys VII so yeah I'd be annoyed too. ...Much like Phantasy Star's RPG series (1-4) being obscure despite being out the same week as Final Fantasy. 

Ahem, yes, rant over, game worth getting? Yes.

These are my impressions after 3 hours. Port details in the last two paragraphs. 

Like Ys Seven, I’m experiencing Memories of Celceta for the first time via its PC port. I’ve played the original Ys 4 both on Snes and PC Engine, and I’m delighted by how good of a job Falcom have done reimagining Ys 4 with this game. Ever since Ys Origin Falcom have aimed for a higher caliber of storytelling in the Ys series, with mixed results. I loved the story in Ys Origin, whereas Ys Seven’s story was a pile of garbage. Ys Memories of Celceta has so far been closer to the quality shown in Ys Origin. Characters have genuine charm, the pace is better and the premise as a whole is more intriguing. I don’t know where the story is going, and I’m interested in finding out what it’s going to do. This isn’t a straightforward remake of Ys 4 like how Ys Oath in Felghana was a remake of Ys 3. This is a more ambitious reimagining of the original game. So even though it has the same music, the same characters, and the same setting as Ys 4, it’s like experiencing it for the first time. I’m happy with what Falcom decided to do with this. The party system introduced in Seven is still a bit visually chaotic, and the mechanics aren't as precise as in Ys 6, Fleghana & Origin. But it plays better than Seven, and I'm not far enough into it to judge it fairly on how well the mechanics scale and sustain across the entire game.

The PC port is good, but not perfect. The biggest issue is the sound volume balance. The balancing of music, ambiance, and SFX isn’t authentic to the Vita original. More importantly, the system sounds are way too loud, like the camp menu and opening chests, and there is no way to adjust these sounds separately. At first, I wasn’t sure how annoying this would be in the long run, but now after 3 hours I can say with certainty it’s bad enough that you can’t get used to it. By default, the voice acting was also disturbingly loud, but you can adjust it with its own slider. But the system menu sounds will blow your ears out every time you decide to save or manage the inventory, and you can’t adjust it.

Apart from the sound mixing, the port is stable and fast. With a Geforce 1070, I’m easily maintaining over 60fps with all the settings maxed out at 4K with 4xMSAA. There are some new effects added to this version, like “HDR”, which in the case of this game is an advanced bloom effect. You can adjust its intensity; I recommend the weak preset for both its settings. The default setting is garish and blows out too much texture detail on characters. If the sound mixing is fixed, this will clearly be the best version of the game. It's already in great shape, as it looks and plays better than the other versions of the game. It's good enough already that I can recommend it as is, even though I'm finding myself grimacing in pain every time I open the menu to save.

Hello friends,

Today i write to you a review about Ys IV: Memories of Celceta. According to forum posts, this game is based on the Mask of the Sun version of the game. Unlike the previous entries in the Ys series, this one has alot of changes going for it that previous games did not. There is now the ability to have a party and control party members, the ability to refine weapons and make them stronger, the ability to find items and resources to make them stronger by exchanging them for better items, and so much more has changed since Ys 3.

If your playing this game in order, this is technically the 4th game in the series. This is not timewise though, nor is it canon order. This game came out much later, in fact it came out quite a bit after the 6th game in the series even. Anyways, here is my pro/con list:

PROS:

- An expanded party with ability to control and switch between party members when controlling them. Ys seven also features the same game mechanics if your playing in cannoncial order.
- The ability to refine equipment in the game, and find resources to upgrade them.
- The great music, which is also found in previous entries of this series.
- Lots of sidequests and even area's to explore off the beaten path.
- Great story for this game.
- Unlockable time trial and harder modes after beating game once.

CONS

- Some of the items and quest items are hard to find sometimes and not really directed to where you find them.
- Mapping is one of the more difficult things to do in the game, and even missing one square inch will make it so you don't get the mapping achievment.
- Having the configuration load everytime when you load up the game can get annoying after awhile. At first, i did not even know it was normal until someone told me it is on the forums.


I really recommend this game if your a fan of the other Ys games, but be aware, there are alot of changes graphic wise and party wise in this game compared to earlier entries into the series. 



NOTE: At the time of this writing, Ys 5 has not been released. If you are playing the games in order on pc, you should play YS 6: The Ark of Napishtim next.

I spent many a happy hour of my younger gaming days with JRPGs – Shining games, older Final Fantasys, Phantasy Star, Terranigma, Secret of Mana, Panzer Dragoon Saga, Lufia, Chorno Tigger etc… like a good Studio Ghibli film, I was always captivated by these games with their colourful characters, interesting world, and that wonderful, almost naïve feeling of going on a grand adventure.  Even when the gameplay mechanics weren’t up to snuff (looking at you Mana!) the storylines, worlds and usually exceptional music always got me through.  However, the genre has really fallen of since its golden days, and although I always crave some of that good JRPG pie, I’m hesitant to pick up modern slices as they tend to be disappointing (final Fantasy 13).  I recently took the plunge with Ni No Kuni 2, which despite looking and sounding gorgeous, struck me as a hollow, boring and rather archaically designed game.  Afterwards, still needing a JRPG fix, I picked this up, a game that was probably made for cheaper than the tea and biscuits budget for Nino Kuni, yet IMHO surpasses it in all the ways that counts.

I’m not too familiar with the YS series, but apparently Celceta is one of the weaker entries.  The other games must be insanely good then, as I had an amazing time with Celceta from start to finish.  While the storyline of the game isn’t exactly Shakespeare and has a lot of clichés (amnesiac hero, forbidden technology of a long dead empire), it propels the gameplay well enough.  I really loved the side quests in the towns though, which are some of the points where the game shines brightest due to the quirky characters.  The game’s ending is a bit of a wet fart but having had such a blast with the game up until that point I was ready to forgive.

Overall, Celceta was just bucket loads of fun.  The gameplay is really fast-paced, as you run (or roll) around exploring, looking for secrets, and smacking the crap out of everything that moves, popping of special moves and hitting perfect dodges and blocks to your hearts content.  Nothing too complex here, but there was a really fast, arcady feel to the combat that stayed fresh for the whole game, and with 6 different characters to swap between, I was happy as a kid in a cake shop. The music is phenomenal, almost like Sonata Arctica / Stratovarious style power metal at times, and while graphically this is a port of an old hand held game, the lack of detail is offset by vibrant colours, smooth animations and great sound effects, and the monsters look pretty cool.  Dungeons are also fairly good, maybe a little too simple, but a couple of them do have some light puzzle elements to break up the combat, and with different artefacts (such as the dwarf bracelet which shrinks you) or each character’s unique skills, there’s just enough complexity to keep it fresh till the end.  All in all, this feels like a lost gem from the PS1 / PS2 era, or like what Secret of Mana might be like if it had combo/dodge heavy combat.

Now, I understand that for many, your mileage will vary depending on just how much nostaligia you hold for JRPGS, and also bare in mind that this is a lower budget title and isn’t gonna measure up to modern AAA titles.  However, if you’re up for a retro JRPG adventure with an ok storyline, madly good combat and a Japanese power metal soundtrack, you might wanna give this a try.  Now, time to check out some more of these Ys games!

I think Ys is one of the best action RPG series out there. I played a bit when I was younger, but I truly discovered it in the past years. All games in the series are worth a playthrough and they all have common qualities, although each game feels unique (even if you play the same character -Adol Christin- in most of them!)

Common strengths of the series are: the consistently excellent music; the quick and exciting gameplay, coupled with satisfying level progression; the relatively small scope of each game, especially before the modern party-based entries; the excellent writing and worldbuilding, including an epic story, strong plot twists and a good amount of cheeky humour.

Here's my personal and very subjective list of what to play in the Ys series. Just know that they are all standalone games, and are not published in chronological order of the story.

**MUST-PLAY TIER
- YS ORIGIN: If you're playing only one, I think it should be this one: as the last game made before modern party-based titles, Origin sits perfectly between Ys eras. The game itself is set centuries before the rest of the series, offering a good understanding of its foundational lore. It also has 3 interwoven stories that work well together, if you're willing to replay the game.

- YS I & II: The games that started it all! They're not my ultimate pick because of the outdated mechanics and high difficulty limiting their accessibility, but all the strong foundations of the future series are there! All the details I love are already there, like the journal with fun 1-paragraph character descriptions, the weapons and armors grid display, the satisfying progression, the killer soundtrack and so on.

- YS IV: MEMORIES OF CELCETA: I love Ys IV, its setting and the organic progression of the plot. Compared to "old Ys", this is one of the longer modern party-based entries, where you control more than one character. It is a re-imagining of an older Ys IV from the 90's, and as such it is the technical successor of Ys Seven.

- YS IX: MONSTRUM NOX: One of the very best in the series, with very strong setting and characters, bringing a surprisingly good story to life. I don't recommend playing it first even if you totally can, since it contains an amazing amount of references to previous games. It is a strong standalone game but is best enjoyed with a deep knowledge of the series.


**SHOULD-PLAY TIER
- YS VI: ARK OF NAPISHTIM: I was surprised how much I enjoyed Ys 6, as it was released a while ago and is technically weaker than Origin and Oath in Felghana, but it has a very strong setting and story. It's not "must-play" for me because of its somewhat unbalanced progression, some plot holes in an otherwise excellent story, and a bland endgame boss.

- YS VIII: LACRIMOSA OF DANA: an absolutely amazing game almost to the very end, until its story and mechanics both crumble under their own weight. It is still very enjoyable and displays all the great qualities of the series, but my interest plummeted sharply during the last hours of grinding and narrative twists. Best soundtrack of the series!

- YS: OATH IN FELGHANA: I don't love this one as much as other people do, but it is a very nice game if you already have love for the series. The unbalanced progression and unfair boss difficulty prevents it from being an instant recommendation for me, but it's also a great reimagining of the old Ys III: Wanderers from Ys on SNES.

- YS SEVEN: I honestly thought I would hate this one, but I was wrong! I love that it comes right after the Ys VI story, including some recurring characters. It is the first of the party-based era of "modern Ys", with somewhat rough but efficient mechanics, and your friend Dogi the wall-breaker as a playable character for the first time! Even with a lot of clichés all around the place, it is still a strong and very satisfying entry.

Alright this is my 3rd Ys game (after Chronicles 1 & 2 and Origin), and I have yet to be disappointed by this series.

The good:
I like the new party system, though I rarely switched over from Adol unless I needed to for certain obstacles.

The conclusion was just fine. I honestly don't know why some people don't seem to like it.

All party members gain experience whether or not they are in your active 3 members.
Lots of unique biomes.

The meh:
Loot and crafting systems are kind of at cross-purposes. I mean you'd be a fool not to add ice and paralysis to nearly every weapon you come across, but that requires gem crafting and then reinforcement.  Which means finding new weapons is less "whee, I found a new weapon" and more "great, now I have to go to a store and do some crafting before I actually use this".
There are a few loose ends to the story - especially in regards to the sexy princess-governor. But I honestly didn't mind.

Unlike many other older JRPGs, playing on Easy is actually *really* easy.  I'm totally in it for the story, but if you prefer your bosses to wipe the floor with you a few times before you figure them out, play Normal.

This was a relatively cozy JRPG that did not have me running to Internet walkthroughs or guides - which is good, sometimes you don't want to overtax your brain. Very accessible and wholesome overall.

To talk about Memories of Celceta it is important to speak of Celceta's journey into modernity. Due to Falcom's incredibly storied history, Adol's adventure in Celceta has always had a layer of uncertainty. To keep it brief, Falcom was approached by Hudson for plans to develop a sequel to Ys III, however, due to poor upper management and mass resignations following Ys I, Ys II and Ys III Falcom was unable to develop a new entry. Due to this, Falcom pursued partnerships with other developers to create a Ys IV sequel for various consoles. Falcom would ultimately provide the framework for Ys IV's scenario (including characters, setting, story, soundtrack, etc.) and allow Hudson and Tonkin Soft to create Ys IV: Dawn of Ys (PC Engine/TurboGrafx-16) and Ys IV: Mask of the Sun (SNES) respectively. 

Then, in 2005 Taito ported Ys IV (along with other Ys titles) to PS2 under the title Ys IV: Mask of the Sun: A New Theory. These three titles all shared similarities in setting, characters, and other aspects of Falcom's original design doc but with a few notable changes such as the primary antagonist. 

Among these, Ys IV: Dawn of Ys was always considered "canonical" due to being released first and Ys IV coming about as a result of Hudson's initial proposal. However, in 2003 Falcom published an official Ys timeline which marked Ys IV: Mask of the Sun as the proper interpretation of Adol's adventure as it closely matched the original design and vision Falcom sought. 

Thankfully though, in 2012 Falcom released their interpretation of Adol's time in Celceta with Ys: Memories of Celceta for the PS Vita. 

This game is the definitive interpretation of Adol's journey in Celceta and was well worth such a turbulent history. Ys: Memories of Celceta is such a treat to play. Memories of Celceta takes the foundation of Ys Seven and elevates it to an entirely new level by refining many of the systems introduced in Ys Seven creating a tighter, more robust experience. In every way, this game surpasses Ys Seven on a technical level. You can tell Falcom critically thought about Ys Seven and the players, and aimed to make a better experience from the map design, to the increasingly thorough map itself, to the material gathering, to the weapon crafting, to the skill design and so much more.

And as per Falcom standard, the story, characters, settings, and soundtracks all remain immensely memorable. There are moments throughout that are inspired by Falcom's love for Ys I + II with locations and camera views that call back so emotionally to Adol's most recent adventure in Esteria. Memories of Celceta also take things one step further by acting to consolidate the Eldeen lore and mythos that were so prominent early on in Adol Christin's journey. This game was crafted with consideration for every aspect of Adol's journey, going so far as to flesh out characters and events that have yet to happen chronologically that we as players have already experienced. Part of Ys' appeal is that Adol Christin's travelogues are told "out of order", as they are discovered, which makes Celceta such an important story to experience. This game is the origin of Adol giving meaning to his journey through the title of "Adventurer" and this incredibly pivotal moment is one that makes this game so beautiful. This, on top of setting the stage for Adol's future encounters. 

In sum, Memories of Celceta is a great game that deserves its place among Adol's travelogue and one that is important to experience as the definitive interpretation of his time in Celceta. It is a game that I love, as I do with every other Ys entry and one that I think is important to play for any fan of Adol's journey.

I recently bought and played Ys8 a short time ago and it was a) excellent and b) reminded me that I actually have a fond spot for this series even though I've only played a couple of the entries. So began my project to work my way through the series and here I am with #4.

It was interesting coming to this having played Ys8 so recently too, since so many of the systems there seem to have gotten their root either here (or perhaps in Seven which I will get to in due course). But it feels less fleshed out and more a prototype of the refinements seen in the newer game. So you get a party of three, each character does one of three types of damage being slash/pierce/strike, and some enemies are only weak to one. There's no "break" here as in Ys8 but doling enough damage with a weakness will stun and let the other party members actually do some damage. Flash Move and Flash Guard are here, one being a just-dodge roll that grants you speedy movemen/enemy slowdown, the other a just-parry that grants a brief bit of 100% crits. Downside is that there's no way to tell when it's going to wear off but you'll get a sense of the timing with experience. There's plenty of skills to assign to suit your playstyle, and Extra Skills granting a huge attack are great for taking down bosses and such. This all works very well and despite some of the crust it controls well overall and smacking enemies around as the loot pinatas they are is satisfying.

Onto the crust. The game is quite ugly by today's standards. This is basically just a resolution upscaled Vita port. It's perfectly serviceable and I don't mind it my self but grafix whores are probably going to be put off by that. The PS4 got the HUD and other UI elements up-rez'd but not this port which is a small bummer. There's no jump button which makes the fact that this game has "air combos" really strange. Camera controls don't exist - it moves on rails per-area, and it actually works pretty well in terms of navigation but combat can get a little frantic and hard to see your party in all the skill effects and stuff, which in turn can make it hard to Flash Move/Guard properly. I never felt any of this to be a deal breaker, but just keep in mind that this game wears it's Vita-ness on its sleeve in these regards. Otherwise the port seems perfectly cromulent: I experienced no crashes, it's happy to alt-tab out of it and the graphical simplicity means even a toaster can run this.

The music, as always, is spectacular. Though having played 8 and 1-3 (I've actually played 3 on TurboCD, SNES and Oath in Felghana so I've heard it a lot) I'd rank this as the weakest of the bunch. It's still excellent though.
