There, it finally happened. Now every main Ys game (apart from the still not remade V) is available on PC for your enjoyment. This latest release is a new canon re-imagining of the fourth entry in the main series, that previously was comprised of two similar, but different games telling a similar story. Oh, the events of the game are also set as a chronological second adventure and happen before the third game (Oath in Felghana) but that doesn't matter. What matters is that the game is fun. Even if not the best in the series.

This is the second game to follow the new gameplay formula introduced in Ys SEVEN, so instead of just playing as Adol (adventurer and the main character of the series), you play as a party of 3 characters, able to switch on the fly. And each of the characters deals a special type of damage, with different enemy types being more susseptable to certain types of damage. As with every game in the series, it is an incredibly fast paced real time action RPG with rather heavy emphasis on exploration and some puzzle solving. Though, one thing, that is actually still unique just to this game, is the fact that you can swim. That's right - not walk under water or on the water, but actually swim. You can even fight underwater and one part of a boss battle uses these swimming controls. Which suck, so I'm not surprised why they were never really used in other Ys games.

Oh and just like in Ys SEVEN you can't jump. Just dodge. Which indeed means that small difference in height can be an impassable block. Can't control the camera as well, with it being mostly isometric. Which is the usual thing for the Ys games, so why bring this up? Well, you see, while Celceta was released on PC just now (at least internationally), it's a game from 2012. Lacrimosa of DANA, which was released on PC earlier this year, is a 2016 game. And what Nihon Falcom has done to the series in just 4 years is staggering. Celceta feels like a pretty SEVEN, the mechanics, the looks, the feel, the story made better. Which was a common template for their releases based on Ark of Napishtim mechanics. Ys VIII feels like what the series have been leading up to, not just "previous game made better", but "entire series perfected". And playing Celceta after VIII just feels slightly disappointing.

I mean, I still could've stop playing, because they indeed made everything introduced in SEVEN work really well. Controls feel better, Flash Guard and Flash Evade are a joy to pull off and you can bind controls in a way that actually makes sense. Though it is obvious from the UI design that a lot of decisions were made specifically for the touch-enabled PS Vita, it still feels perfectly fine with a gamepad. The damage type concept feels great, where in SEVEN it often became annoying. Gathering resources is fun and probably even less grindey than it is in VIII. Exploring the map is fun. Interface is clean. Story starts in a bit of a frustrating tutorial-ish way, and hits a bit too many staples of the series, but is actually fun. Not as engaging as VIII, but with some nice characters and cool scenes. Hell, this game might have one of the most interesting ending act sequences of events I've seen in the series.

But it's just not there yet, not where it will become with VIII. Map completion percentage, for example, is ridiculous and wants you to hug every playable area wall on the open world. Though, it seems that if you just complete the game (past the point where the percentage matters unless you then go to NG+ and you can), but the dialogue for getting the completion is there for the normal pre-ending part. The concept for the special skills per character is annoying, since to use one you have to switch to said character and if they're not in the party you go to menu, switch character in, do this one-time skill use, go to menu and switch your usual party back in. Special skill uses pop up at rather random locations and depending on with whom you prefer to play (and for whom you bought the best equipment) those areas just become a drag due to the constant switching. Oh and the character voice over barks, especially for some bosses, are overdone. No one wants you to burn to the ground all the time, but it's still grating. Also, some sounds (and ambience in some locations) seems to be mixed badly and can be loud or inappropriate. And speaking of sound, the music in this entry is, while as usual for Falcom not bad, just isn't as great as it could be, with some locations having really boring tunes.

Again - I did love playing the game. It is one of the Ys games to definitely check out if you haven't played the series or if you are interested in them, but casually. But if you're looking for the absolute best of the series, I'd rather suggest checking Origin, Oath in Felghana and, of course, the absolutely fantastic VIII. If I had to continue the list, Celceta would probably be next. I enjoyed my time with it a lot. It's just a bit of a shame that I've experienced VIII before playing this game.

Unfortunately, it's also the entry I would also consider to be one of the weakest in the series. A relatively boring first half of the game, uninspired bosses, and various other steps back from Ys: Lacrimosa make this, ultimately, nothing more than an average to below average entry, buoyed by an interesting cast and a much more interesting second half, though with a disappointing, unsatisfying ending.

Celceta is the 3rd entry in the Seven Engine games, along with Ys Seven and Ys: Lacrimosa of Dana. The game is much closer to Seven in gameplay than Lacrimosa, with no jumping, only dodge rolls, and a static camera. It maintains the "3-level skills" progression, and an auto-charging SP gain attack, and the ability to swap Adol out of the party, but is otherwise almost identical to 7. Most of the characters fight identically to others in the games, in function if not in name. There are two characters of each damage type (Slash, Strike, Pierce), one male, one female, and as in the other games, enemies are weak to one damage type and resistant to others, though this function becomes less prominent later on as strong enemies are equally damaged by all types. Skills and Extra skills are used and spammed with wild abandon to level them up, and will be the bulk of your damage for the entire game. The party members were all useful at times, and each party member has a unique field skill that makes you use everyone for at least a little bit. These areas are generally accompanied by enemies weak to that party member's damage type as well. The game has the same "map exploration" game long sidequest that Lacrimosa does, but doesn't have the area by area breakdown of map completion, rather, it only has a total overworld percentage. If you're stuck at 99.7%, your only hope is to stare at the map, hope you see a tiny little shaded out area, and run around wall hugging all of the forests, hoping you tick the last percentage points.

Bosses were disappointing affairs, and the game's reliance on Flash Guard and Flash Move becomes especially noticeable lategame, where almost every boss has a massive attack that either can or cannot be stunned out of, and getting hit by it results in a multi hit hundreds of damage per tick attack that generally instantly kills the character you're using unless you Flash Dodge or Flash Guard it. Other earlier bosses can be absolutely destroyed by standing in front of it, Flash Guarding, and then spamming attacks and skills, Flash Guarding as needed, oftentimes single or 2 cycling the boss from full HP to nothing. This was a definite change from other games, even Lacrimosa which at least required you to move, dodge, and understand attacks, even if you were an extremely proficient Flash Guarder.

The music and graphical presentation are on par with the other Ys games. The music is what you'd expect (but again, didn't rank extremely highly on my lsit of Ys games music) and the graphics are a midpoint between Seven and Lacrimosa.

The story is not the game's strong suit, unlike Lacrimosa or Seven, which told relatively interesting (if a little cliche in Seven's case) stories. Celceta's centers on the return of Adol's memories, but the more interesting ones about Adol's childhood are skimmed over in favor of memories that are immediately rendered obsolete because the thing they're talking about is answered in the next 5 minutes, giving no real mystery or intrigue. There are links to Ys I and II, Origins, Oath, and Napishtim, which are nice to see, but none of them play any role in the game's actual plot besides being interesting mentions. The Oath references here are of special note, since the game makes a very big deal out of a particular monster type that ends up being absolutely nothing but a single monster type that requires Adol to kill it after it's stunned. The end of the game is very sudden and leaves a billion open questions hanging, and the game's explanation of "maybe this was the deeper meaning all along" is not satisfying in the least. It's as though they just decided to not make an epilogue or do anything after the final boss.

Overall, the game is still an enjoyable Ys adventure, so I'll recommend it mostly as a fan,and to fans of the series... but it goes on the bottom of the list for sure, having played every single Ys game to completion now. A pass for anyone not a fan of the series, but I suppose at this point, you'd played them all or you've played none of them - and if you haven't played any of them, this isn't the place to start. For that, I'd suggest Ys: Origins, Ys: Oath in Felghana, or Ys: Lacrimosa of Dana, instead.

This was my first Falcom game that I originally played several years ago on the Vita. I only got about 10 hours in then dropped it for other games at the time. Now, having finished the game, I feel confident in saying that it was fun but does have some issues.

First, the story. I've been working my way through the Ys series and so far, I've finished I, II, Origin, and now Celceta. Comparing the story of Celceta to the others, I can't help but feel underwhelmed. The characters are generally pretty well written, with some exceptions. But the pacing of the story is off. Especially towards the end of the game, which felt rushed.

Second, the gameplay. This is the real fun part of the game for me and why I play Ys. I found flash guarding and flash dodging awkward but serviceable. The combat overall was fun and a little more involved than Origins, although it did get repetitive by the end of the game as there were certain skills I just didn't even bother using. Additionally, the upgrade system seems almost worthless considering how often you get new gear. 

Third, the map and collection garbage. The game takes place in a linear world map that opens up as you progress. This is fine especially as you get the ability to teleport around, greatly reducing the amount of travel time, which is much appreciated. However, one of the main collection aspects of the game is 100% map completion. It's been noted in other reviews but the map percentage algorithm is not great. I finished the game with a 99.6% map completion as I was unable to find the little bit of map I haven't uncovered. This, combined with other collection crap like "open all chests" and "mine all resource points" are ridiculous grinds that make the game more tedious and less fun. The rewards aren't worth it either, beyond the achievements, except for the map completion which gives you the final artifact you need to complete the "collect all the things" achievement. How fun... This shouldn't surprise anyone though as Falcom tends to have very grindy collection achievements and gameplay elements in their games. They aren't explicitly necessary but they are there and I find them annoying.

Lastly, bosses and dungeons. Comparing the boss fights and dungeon design to Origins, I am vastly disappointed. Most boss fights, including the final boss fight, boil down to "spam attacks, build SP, stun boss, use EX, heal when low on health, repeat until boss is dead". It's a simple formula that doesn't ever change all that much. You can mix it up with flash guards and dodges but the core loop is the same. This repetitive nature applies to the dungeons too, unfortunately. Some of them are fun to explore, even if they are linear, as they require you to switch characters to use certain abilities, like Karna's knife throwing or Ozma's ability to break cracks in walls. Other dungeons are tedious and annoying, requiring you to do some weird backtracking just to get a chest that didn't even have a good item in it. 

Overall, I recommend this game to Ys fans if you know what you're getting into. It has some good ideas and I like that I was able to finish it in less than 30 hours but just know that it does have several weak spots and can be a bit of a grind.

Ys: Memories of Celceta – “Map the World, Save the World, Forget Why You're Doing Either”

Adol Christin wakes up in the middle of a forest with no memory, no gear, and no idea how he got there—which is oddly relatable. Within minutes, someone hands him a magical GPS and says, “Go touch every tree in the forest.” And he does. For 30 hours.

Combat is fast, flashy, and fun—if a bit button-mashy. You’ve got dodges, blocks, and anime flourishes galore. The party-switching system returns from Ys Seven, letting you cycle through characters like you’re speed-scrolling a gacha roster. None of them can jump, by the way. Not even a hop. Adventurers, grounded by design.

The story? Starts strong with amnesia intrigue and then sort of... forgets to be interesting. The villains appear, monologue, and die like bad cosplay at a fan convention. Character development peaks right when someone joins the party and never again. But hey, at least they're charming anime clichés.

Mapping the overworld is the big gimmick here, and it's great—if you love manually rubbing against every suspicious rock face like you’re trying to unlock a romance subplot with the environment. The game calls it “exploration.” I call it “arboreal foreplay.”

Visually, it's... a Vita game. With bloom. So much bloom. The camera is locked tighter than Adol’s facial expressions. But the soundtrack? Certified banger status, as always. Falcom’s composers are still working overtime to make sure you’re headbanging while you’re lost in shrubbery.

Despite its janky camera, undercooked plot, and tree-heavy cartography, Memories of Celceta is a janky, lovable time. It’s like comfort food made by someone who occasionally forgets how to cook—but the seasoning (combat, music, and classic Ys vibes) is just right. I rolled my eyes a lot, but I also played it to the end and had a damn good time doing it.

Another year, another good Ys port from the fine folks at XSEED. Clearly Hyde Inc. was able to learn from their growing pains from their first port -- Ys SEVEN -- because as far as I can tell, there were significantly less issues with MoC on launch than its predecessor. The folks over at NIS America could learn a thing or two from this port -- the best I've heard from someone defending the Ys VIII PC port was that in "only" crashed 15 times during 50 hours of gameplay. You want to know how many times MoC crashed on me? Zero. Granted, I started playing the game roughly a week after launch, so I may have benefited from some later patches.

Memories of Celceta is an interquel, taking place between Ys II and Oath in Felghana. It's Falcom's own take on Ys IV, which was previously farmed out to two other companies -- Tonkin House's downright mediocre Mask of the Sun for the Super Famicom, which was considered canonical by Falcom until MoC came out and Alfa System's The Dawn of Ys for the PC Engine, generally considered the best of the bump combat-style Ys games. Of course, neither of these versions came out in North America or Europe in any official capacity, so MoC gets the edge on that front.

The game starts with Adol wandering around the town of Casnan, having completely lost his memory. He stumbles his way into the local inn before collapsing. Once he recovers, he makes the acquaintanceship of Duren, an information broker, who decides to help Adol, as he has a reputation for finding adventure (and therefore, useful information). Soon after, they are tasked by the local governess Griselda to explore and map out the mysterious forests of Celceta. Throughout the journey, Adol is reintroduced to people he met on his previous journey (one he has unfortunately forgotten) and finds many mysterious artifacts, stumbling upon another world-ending crisis as he often does.

Memories of Celceta runs on a refined version of Ys SEVEN's engine, thus the party system from the previous game returns. This game also manages to add a new defense mechanic: the "Flash Move". If the player's character is able to dodge an enemy attack at a specific moment, the enemies onscreen slowdown for a brief period, similar to Bayonetta's Witch Time. Unlocking new special attacks is also different from the previous game, they're obtained by defeating a set number of "difficult" enemies. Frankly, I think I preferred the old system. The original release also included various touch puzzles that exploited the Vita's touch screen and touchpad, but later updates allowed them to be performed with standard controls (to make the game compatible with PSTV). The PC version allows players to use their mouse or the controller, which is a nice touch.

XSEED and Hyde did a much better job on the graphics this time around, managing to even offset the filters present in the original Vita version of the game -- though a similar bloom option is available in the game. On top of that, they managed to even exceed (ha ha!) Ys SEVEN's 60 FPS, offering 120 frames per second and even uncapped, though the latter isn't particularly recommended.

So just like the previous game (and every other Ys game XSEED's released on here), I'd recommend you pick it up if you're in the mood to play a damn fine action RPG. As with the previous game, it's a little on the easy side -- I did my first run on Hard Mode, just like with SEVEN.

Most things are initially a mystery and you have to progress to gain a good understanding of the situation. The colourful cast of characters helps, as does a good translation.

--STORY--
Ys: Memories of Celceta is an HD remake of Ys 4, and thus chronologically it's in the middle of the storyline for the Ys series. In it's own self-contained bubble, the story of Celceta isn't anything grand. Unlike some other Ys games, Celceta's story merely has its own story and goes with it instead of adding any grand expansion to the Ys world's lore. However, this doesn't mean it's a bad story, the story is very fun and has it's own unique twists that are nice to experience, especially near the final phase of the game.

In order to completely appreciate Celceta's story it is recommended to play previous released Ys titles as it makes lore nods and references which made the Ys fan in me go "Oh wow that's just like ____!" and so forth. It's not mandatory, but it adds a lot to the experience.

--GAMEPLAY--
The Ys series is known for it's fast, skill-based action-packed gameplay and Falcom did a great job here. Ys Celceta builds off of the Party-Based System which was first introduced in Ys Seven back in 2009. Adol is not the sole playable character, but instead one of many as you'll pick up several playable characters with their own unique styles of combat. Each character has their own set of skills that you can map to the skill buttons, and they learn several more skills as you continue playing. Skills can combo off of one another and depending on how skilled you are you can crate some nifty combos.

Furthermore, Ys Celceta has a very fun dodge/block mechanic that reminds me of Bayonetta. If you dodge at the right time, time will slow down allowing you to get more hits in, and if you block at the right time you nullify damage and deal critical damage for a certain period of time, it's very skill-based is a shining point of the game's gameplay. Overall it's extremely fluid and fun.

My only complaint about the gameplay is its use of items. There are items for pretty much any status effect and you can stack wayyyy too many HP potions which can trivialize the game, assuming you farm the money to buy that many pots to begin with. So I suggest limiting yourself if possible.

--OTHER TIDBITS--
Ys Celceta can run at 60 FPS if your rig can handle it, it has a lot of graphic customizable options that will also let lower-end systems play it (like mine, lol). 

You can save virtually anywhere in this game which makes it extremely friendly to play in short or long bursts alike. 

The voice acting is pretty good as you have a lot of talented VAs like Bryce Papenbrook, Cristina Vee, Wendee Lee, and so forth. 

The music is simply stunning, Falcom is known for their music and it really shines here.

And the graphics while not the best are definitely serviceable, especially with this port that allows the game to look far better than it did on the VITA.

--OVERALL--
Solid entry in the Ys series, every Ys fan has to play this game and overall a great Action RPG experience that will last you anywhere between 25-30 hours of gameplay on a first playthrough.

First party system Ys game I've played so far, and I've been having a ton of fun with it. Going to finish this review once I finish my first playthrough.

EDIT: Finished the game. Here are my thoughts:

[b]Gameplay:[/b] For my first party system Ys game, this was pretty different from what I was expecting, but as much as I would've preferred the Napishtim battle system with party members, I still found it really satisfying. All of the party members felt really really fun to use, though they and their skills did feel a bit unbalanced at times. I found myself frequenty cycling between them just to mix things up. Normal difficulty is pretty easy compared to the other Ys games I've played so far, though I haven't tried any higher difficulties yet. Didn't struggle with any of the bosses except the Sacred Beast's Lair one (came in underequipped, still beat it underequipped), Gadis, and the Silver Area boss. Getting new equipment and raising your level is still important in this game, but not nearly to the same extent as the Napishtim engine games. I never needed to grind at any point in my playthrough; you won't need to as long as you're attacking enemies as you go along. You can safely ignore tempering your gear this time around, though it does give you some neat stat bonuses. The forced autotargeting is a double-edged sword, since it occasionally gets the wrong target or interferes in certain spots. The game gives you some dialogue options at points, but they don't have an impact on the story or your party; the most you're getting is usually different flavor text or a funny response. Be warned that map completion REQUIRES you to hug the walls - simply filling in the exploreable space isn't enough.

[b]Graphics:[/b] The game's a port of a PS Vita title that had mediocre visuals even for that console's standards, so don't expect top-notch visual quality. Object lighting's been SADX'd compared to the Vita original and the default bloom setting is obscenely strong by default compared to the other versions. It also lacks the higher resolution textures and improved particle/water effects from the "Kai" remaster on PS4, though the texture filtering options do look better. The biggest visual advantage over the other versions is support for high framerates and high resolutions. The environments do look pretty despite the overall visual fidelity, but the character models have a lot of jaggies and are shaded a bit oddly. They don't always match the artwork, either, though I think I actually prefer Adol's in-game design. Animations are pretty stiff.

[b]Sound:[/b] As usual with the Ys series, the soundtrack is top-notch overall. I feel like some of the arrangements of the original Ys IV-era Falcom jdk team compositions are a bit weak, though, and a few of my favorites were outright missing (e.g. Valley of Quicksand, Beyond Reminiscence). The new tracks are top-notch, however. Sound effects are pretty satisfying. A lot of them are recognizable from previous Falcom games. Favorite tracks: (New) Ancient Land, The Moment After the Storm, Forest of Dawn, Black Wings (Arranged) Burning Sword, Tower/Iris, Ancient Kingdom, The Final Decisive Battle

[b]Performance:[/b] Being a port of a Vita title, you wouldn't expect to need a supercomputer to run this, and sure enough, I had no issues running this on a potato. Tested this on a few different systems. My gaming desktop (Ryzen 5600G, RTX 2080S) was able to run this at 1440p60 at max settings (didn't try 120 to avoid bugs, don't have a 4K monitor in that room), my main laptop (i7-11800H, RTX 3060M) pushed 4K60 on high, and one of my potato laptops (Pentium Silver N5000) was able to keep a mostly stable 30FPS on low settings with some dips in the last dungeon.

[b]Story:[/b] Ys isn't a series that you play for the story, though I liked Celceta's story overall. It's not my favorite in the series. I liked the character interactions, but the writing overall isn't up to part with the rest of the series. The townsfolk don't feel nearly as fleshed out as the Napishtim engine games or even I&II Eternal. I also have to agree that the ending is the worst in the series that I've gone through so far. It gets cut off extremely abruptly, deliberately leaving a lot of unanswered questions. I didn't let that hamper my enjoyment of the rest of the game, though. Story usually comes second in Ys anyway.

In spite of my issues with this game, it was enough to hook me right back into the series just as I was starting to feel burnt out. Would definitely recommend overall.

On its own, [i]Memories of Celceta[/i] is a decent game and a fine entry into the [i]Ys[/i] series. For those familiar with [i]Ys IV: Mask of the Sun[/i] (SNES version) and/or [i]Ys IV: Dawn of Ys[/i] (PC Engine version) which were both released in Japan only, [i]Memories[/i] offers a lot of nostalgia and references to both. The story itself is a pastiche of both games' plots mixed to create something altogether new.

The game draws more on [i]Dawn of Ys[/i] in terms of music, level design, and character design but heavily on [i]Mask[/i] for the central premise. Unlike both previous games, players will not need to be intimately familiar with the first two [i]Ys[/i] games to understand what's going on. Though it does make references to events in those as well as events in both previous [i]Ys IV[/i] incarnations (a memory of Calilica referencing Promalock/Promarock, a memory of Dogi telling Adol not to get locked up in prison, both of which happen in both previous [i]Ys IV[/i] games). Likewise, the option to call Leeza "Lilia" is a reference to a character from [i]Ys II.[/i]


Unfortunately, the decision to go with an all new story and divorcing it from the first two [i]Ys[/i] games does mean certain things from both previous [i]Ys IV[/i] games have been cut completely. Like the ability to revisit characters from both or return to Lance/Rance Village and learn what's happened in the two years since the end of [i]Ys II.[/i]

Celceta is a solid Action RPG built on top of a failed story.

Celceta is Falcom's version of Ys IV. The originals were made by other game developers with Falcom's input. However, comparing Celceta to the original Ys IV games is like comparing apples to cheese. The similarities are there, but other than the few obvious ones (apples and cheese are both food), it's almost impossible to make the connections without deep thought and intimate knowledge of all 3 versions of Ys IV.

Celcela's strongest point is its gameplay, which is a solid improvement over previously developed Ys Seven. Highlights include the new Flash Move, a revamped method of learning Skills, an improved crafting system, etc. However, the Party System games are already quite easy -- the addition of near unlimited healing items make Celceta one the easiest if not the easiest game in the series (that is currently on Steam).

The new mapping mechanic, though an interesting idea, stands out as being a rather rough first iteration, requiring wall hugging in order to properly map everything -- fortunately, it's completely optional to 100% the map, and will probably be a better overall experience by not worrying about doing so.

For the most part, the bosses are a strong point of the game, being fast paced and constantly a threat. But unlike most Ys games, there are a at least 2 bosses in the game that are simply not fun to fight -- they are long and boring. In the entire Ys series, there is only one other boss I can think of that meets this criteria.

The music is another strong point. However. Many of the tracks written for the original 2 versions of Ys IV are outright missing from Celceta, well over 10 in fact. With that said, the tracks that are unique to Celceta are solid additions.

Celceta's biggest issues are its story and lore. Strictly speaking, the lore feels almost like a poorly made copy of Napishtim's lore, with some new dressing to make it seem different. In comparison, the lore of the originals is far more unique and interesting, and are the Ys equivalent to the search for "El Dorado". It's also worth noting that the South American styled pyramid structures so prevalent in the original 2 games is almost nowhere to be seen in Celceta.

Celceta's story falls apart. The motivations of the villains is never explained. Because of this, the actions of the villains make zero sense. This drags down the entire story. It is also worth noting that one of the highlight of the original versions of Ys IV, the reveal of the Lost City, is nowhere to be found in Celceta. In fact, there is nothing of the same impact in Celceta. Despite this, the story (broken as it is) is presented well, with plenty of fun little nods to the originals for anyone that played them.

[Ys IV: Mask of the Sun] is one of the worst Ys games I've ever played. And yet, it somehow has a more exciting and overall satisfying story than Celceta, despite Mask of the Sun's atrocious presentation of so many story beats (some of which are downright comically bad).

[Ys IV: Dawn of Ys] is one of the best Ys games I've ever played, taking the bump combat and magic system of Ys I and II, and elevating it to new heights. It's story and lore are superior to Celceta's, despite being a shorter game. Though not cannon, it is remains best version of Ys IV to date.

This game is hard to put down once you start playing because the combat is so addictive. Battle is fast and fluid, character controls are very responsive, skills are fun to use, switching between characters is optional but recommended because the characters all have their own individual combat styles and strengths against different enemies.

If you've ever played Zelda Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom, the combat system will feel familiar as it has the same style of flurry rush dodging and perfect parry blocking. Dodge at the last minute and time will slow down, allowing you to move around and attack faster. Block at the last second, and you will completely nullify the incoming damage and be granted a 100% critical strike buff for a few seconds. The timing window for the blocking feels more lenient than the dodging, which is great because with a bit of practice you can go right up in the enemy's face and trade blows while dishing out massive amounts of damage. It's very gratifying to run up to an enemy that is 10+ levels higher than you and whittle it down with skilful timing of your attacks and blocks.

You control 1 character at a time in a battle party of 3 characters, among 6 playable characters overall. The other two characters are computer controlled and will use their own attacks and abilities on their own, you can command them to play aggressively or defensively with the push of a single button, and you can instantly swap control of the active player-controlled character with a button press. Characters are swappable into and out of the party on the fly and equipment/skills can all be changed mid combat in the menu.

The negatives I found with the game are:
1. There are a *lot* of tutorial popups at the beginning of the game that explain the game systems / shops / skills / combat / party mechanics,
2. The ending is very abrupt, you get a tiny amount of exposition and the game's done, and
3. If you want credit for 100% exploration of the map (quest objective in-game), you literally have to hug the edges of the explorable areas to reveal the fog of war outside of the walkable map areas.

That being said, the tutorials are easy enough to skip through and if you forget the mechanics, there's a screen in the menu to show you a list of the mechanics tutorials and their descriptions. And the rest of the game is honestly so good that none of these issues took away from my enjoyment of the game in the slightest.

Not as good as Ys: I, II, III, and Origins, but still good.

Background: I played Ys III on Super Nintendo (not knowing what it was) as a child and then, decades later, have played the games in order from Origins a few years ago to I and II last year, then III recently, and now IV.  Origins was a fast-paced action game that I thoroughly enjoyed; I credit it for getting me into playing more difficult games or difficulties because the boss battles are difficult at first but beatable eventually.  I thought that I would not like I and II because of the “bump” combat, but it actually worked surprisingly well and I loved the style from Nintendo-era games.  III (Oath of Felghana) was a great recreation of III in 3D, and I enjoyed it.

Ys IV is a PS Vita game, and even on PC it feels like it.  It has the feeling of a handheld action RPG—it feels like a game that you play in a car where the plot is straightforward (map out the forest), you can save any time, you hack and slash your way through the world, and you have the occasional points where you buy new equipment or fight bosses.  For some reason, it feels pretty cookie-cutter compared to the other games that, while similar to other games of the same genre, always seemed to have uniqueness like crazy boss battles, a killer soundtrack, and/or fun characters and adventures.  It took me several hours to get into it.  That said, I eventually began to like it—specifically, for the story and characters.  But it took a while.

The Positives:
-The characters get very good after a few hours.  For example, Duren starts off like kind of a jerk, but then his dialogue becomes decent and you find out more about him that makes him more human and 3-dimensional.  I ended up liking Karna the most (other than Adol), and I enjoyed playing as her a lot with her long-range attacks and cool special abilities.  The other characters, from Ozma to Calilica to Freida, are fine and play their roles in the story just fine.  I miss Dogi, but the reason he’s not in this is because Adol shows up in a town and doesn’t remember anything (and so it makes sense).

-The story gets good as well.  At first, because you don’t know what’s going on, you just take on a quest to map out a forest and so it feels so much like the gameplay is showing and it doesn’t feel so much like anything other than a generic PS Vita game.  But once you get new characters and a reason to be concerned as to what’s happening in the world (e.g., poisoned water supply, sister looking for a brother), it gets more interesting.  And then you uncover some secrets and things become engaging.  My favorite part was how Adol was recognized at each town and shenanigans would ensue (though it happened twice back to back and was confusing for a moment until the dialogue called it out).

-The combat is fun and interesting—your abilities feel powerful, you level up a lot from area to area, and you barely have enough gold to keep up with the weapon and armor upgrades without a little bit of grinding (or returning regularly to get exploration-based rewards from Griselda).  The skills all have three tiers and get subtly better as you develop them.

-The bosses aren’t too bad—they are part classic Ys where they have long, drawn-out combat mechanics, part spam-attack-and-dodge kind of bosses.  I found that on Normal mode, you can eventually just spam-attack and switch between the three characters to win most of them without using healing items; I’m sure that higher difficulties require more finesse than that, though.

The Negatives:
-This game felt long and took a while to get into.  You’ll have to make it about 3-4 hours before it gets you engaged, which might be longer than some people would be willing to do.  It took tens of hours to beat, which felt long for this type of game that typically can be completed in around 20+.  Also, what is the deal with a PS Vita game taking that long?  Just weird overall that the length contrasts so much with the pick-up-and-play-on-a-handheld-for-an-hour-or-two gameplay structure that they were going for.

-The difficulty spikes are noticeable occasionally.  An average enemy takes a while to beat early on until it becomes easy after a while (through leveling and upgraded weapons), but then you’ll go to the next area and become terrible again—because it’s sort of open world in nature, you can run into different areas that are more or less difficult.  So I ended up playing an area that was a little more difficult early and had one of my characters die (I could make it back to the teleportation stones no problem, though) a couple of times or have trouble fighting…and then I’d upgrade my equipment and go to an easier area via a different order and it’d be easy.  By the end, I’d be leveling 10 levels in 40 minutes and then fight bosses without too much difficulty (especially when I learned the “fight until near-death, switch characters, and keep fighting until they’re dead” method to boss fighting).  So it was very strange compared to other Ys games where the leveling was more even (bad->good->great->new area->new weapons->okay->good->great->repeat).

-Much of the game was just mindless hack-and-slash battles with the exception of the occasional high-HP monster in the forest that added an interesting dynamic (and could kill you if you weren’t careful, which was interesting).

-I didn’t like that I had to do a lot of backtracking and revisiting old towns for new quests.  There are also a lot of timed quests (where you have to complete them before the next story point) that you don’t even know exist unless you revisit all of the towns after each boss.  I did that a little (and got up to like ~80% of quests or so), but it just got to be so much of a chore to complete a stage of the game and then go teleport and recheck every town to see what was new that I just didn’t bother (even though I bothered to go back to get some money to afford all of the accessories, etc.).  This is just one of those we-made-an-achievement-for-everything-to-keep-completionists-busy-for-100-hours kinds of things that I didn’t care for at all and just felt like it was a lot of busywork.  The worst part is that there’s an achievement for getting all of the weapons, and you can’t even accomplish it in a single play through because you get temporary weapons during a quest line and can only select one.  So I would just turn off trying to be a completionist for this game unless you love it, but it’s just so long and padded that I just wanted to finish it and move on to the next game.

-Note that you shouldn’t alt-tab out of the game before saving, as I lost over an hour of progress doing so.  My mistake, so I don’t blame the game, but just a warning.

Overall, I enjoyed the game, but it took a while to do so.  I really had to take a few hours to get through the early parts so the story would happen and give myself goals of completing the quests for money, getting the best artifacts, and leveling up my skills to keep myself mentally busy.  I got all of the skills up to level 3, which took up most of the game to do (I used the artifacts that let you get +1, 2, 3, and 4 experience per use, which saves you a ton of time).  The characters you get eventually become cool and the story becomes interesting, but you really have to hang in there.  Definitely the worst of the series that I’ve played thus far, but since I like the series so much it’s still better than other games I’ve played.  It just felt like a generic game of the genre, and for an Ys game that is kind of an insult because I usually like them more than I enjoyed this one.  Still decent, just not as good as the others (maybe unless you’re new to the genre and it’ll be new and interesting to you).

Ys: Memories of Celceta has been my favorite Ys game since it introduced me to the series 4 years ago, and this PC port absolutely does not disappoint. 

Pros:

-Combat is as fluid as ever. This game is a 3D Action RPG in which you have a party of 3 characters, taking control of the lead, and two AI controlled partners whom you can switch to with the press of a button. Some tweaks were made to the system from Ys Seven, such as a rewarding flash-dodge option which allows you to slow time for a couple seconds and fire off a bunch of shots, as well as consolidating perfect-guards into a single button. Each of the 6 playable characters are fun to play as and have their own little nuances that make them fun and add replayability. I know Ys 8 touched on the system a little bit more, but given that that game has a shaky-at-best PC port, I don't have the ability to do a thorough comparison. Point is this game is very fun to play for its entire duration.

-Music is pure bliss, with Falcom JDK doing what they do best. Most of the soundtrack is rockin, either by arranging tunes from the old school (SNES/PCE) Ys IV games which this title is based on, or just some killer new tracks.

-Movement is super fluid and fun, with a ridiculous dodge roll, as well as the single greatest item in the history of Action RPGs about halfway in, which is the Gale Shoes. Put them on and suddenly you become Sonic the damn Hedgehog in terms of movement speed. It also controls surprisingly well, allowing you to tap the sprint button and change direction immediately. I don't know who thought of this idea but it's fun running around like a maniac.

-Xseed added a lot of quality of life upgrades to this port, such as allowing for more options in control customization (although forcing the "talk to people" command on the attack button rather than it being linked to the confirm button is a change from the Vita version I wish wasn't made), having Boss Rush modes, easier save files, a super fast forward button to speed through cutscenes, and so on. In addition they are adding some quality of life patches to improve the game even more.

Cons:

-[strike]Volume balancing still needs work. Super attacks cause the character voices to spike in volume, and sound effects are either a bit too loud or way too quiet, without much in between (I swear the difference between 5 and 6 on this is much bigger than it should be). Still a solid game to listen to, the port just needs a couple tweaks in this area.[/strike] this has been fixed in a patch.

-The bosses in this game aren't as memorable or distinct as in some of the earlier Ys games. 

-Your party AI is generally not very good. They don't always do what you want and there isn't exactly a good way to direct them, as you have only two options for settings (Attacking and Evasive), and they only do about 40% of the damage the player-controlled character does. They're mostly there to have someone to switch to to cover enemy weapon weaknesses or get yourself out of a jam by switching to them. 

So-So:

-The story isn't particularly good, and I did prefer some aspects of the SNES Ys IV to this reimagining of Ys IV. That said, Ys games generally don't do much with their stories anyways, as they are a better source of world-building and lore as opposed to their main plotlines. With Celceta, the story is basically enough to get you through the game, while there's plenty to explore for Ys fans interested in the lore aspect. This is probably the Ys game that actually focuses the most on who Adol actually is in the entire series, and some of the subplots are pretty cool.

-[strike]Would be nice to have dual-audio, however licensing hell sadly is a thing, so they were unable to get the JP audio. There isn't much in the way of voiceover in this game and the English is fine anyways though.[/strike] added in a patch.

-This is probably the easiest Ys game of the ones on PC. While Hard and Nightmare are still a decent challenge, this game doesn't quite hit those notes that earlier Ys games might in this regard for difficulty enthusiasts. Some people like easier, which is fine. I'd say this game is best served as an introduction to the series for someone who might not feel so inclined to start with the more dated Ys I+II and wants to play a more modern-looking game than Origin.

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#369 out of 612)... it's time for Ys (IV): Memories of Celceta.

I've said it before, I'll say it again: Falcom has never made a bad game. Ys: Memories of Celceta is no exception. If you've played any Ys game before, you know what to expect: a fun ARPG with lots of combat and exploration and a simple, but nonetheless compelling story set in a fantasy world heavily inspired by real-world history and mythology. The joy of an Ys game, usually, lies in the invigorating, fast-paced hack-and-slash gameplay.

Memories of Celceta marks the Ys series' second foray into fully 3-dimensional action combat, and while it's certainly an improvement over Ys Seven, the new perspective still doesn't feel quite as polished or satisfying as the older games' sprite-based 2D visuals. Essentially you're engaging with fewer enemies at a time, and it's a bit harder to gauge your distance to foes. Combat remains fast-paced, however, and watching monsters exploded into money and items is as bizarrely thrilling in Celceta as elsewhere. The move to 3D may not improve the combat, but it does improve the exploration aspect of the game—areas have never been bigger. And the 3D map makes navigating these expansive areas relatively painless.

Memories of Celceta also differs from prior games in that it devotes much more time and energy to its narrative—the story told isn't exactly groundbreaking, but it is sufficiently compelling to drive the gameplay and is substantially elevated by Falcom's ever-exceptional musical score.

Note: Also played on Sony Playstation Vita.

Memories of Celceta represents the 4th version of the 4th Y's game, and the only one Falcom themselves developed. Every other version was an outside company following Falcom's design doc, and altering the story to varying degrees. So MoC can be judged in different ways, including as a version of Ys 4 and as an Ys game in general.

	As a version of Ys 4, it's the canon version of the story. All versions of Ys 4 deal with the same general idea (GENERAL spoilers for this game ahead): there existed a race of winged beings (Eldeen) long ago who created powerful masks. These masks, in one way or another, led to the end of the ancient kingdom of Celceta. And these masks are once more being sought after, now by a nefarious trio. Central to the masks is the last remaining member of the Eldeen race, who resides in a village that worships him.

	In MotS (the SNES version of Ys 4), the ancient Eldeen kingdom of Celceta fell after the (evil) Eldeen race lost its war against the humans (who they were attempting to enslave). The humans took the masks as a trophy, and the kingdom submerged beneath the land. The last Eldeen being seeks the masks once more for power/revenge with his 3 cohorts.

	In Dawn (Turbografx version), Celceta was instead a human kingdom which was gifted the masks by the benevolent Eldeen race. The humans intentionally submerged the kingdom as a final resort in thwarting a villain's attempts at obtaining the masks. The last Eldeen being is once again a baddie being assisted by a trio, but in this version the trio is using him to resurrect their leader.

Dawn is the best 'classic' version of the tale, but it plays so different to MoC that you can only compare the story. And it compares favorably to this version. I liked how Dawn tied back to Ys 1 by having the final boss of Ys 1 be the reason for Celceta's submerging. But I also like how MoC ties into the current Ys Falcom lore, even if it isn't as creative.

	When judged in comparison to the franchise the game also fares well. Specifically, Ys 7, which began the play style that MoC continues. A system where you control a party of 3 and switch between them on the fly. Just as Ys7,  you have an attack button that fills up an SP gauge, which is used for special attacks that fill up an 'Extra' Gauge. Which unleashes a powerful move.

	A small change I really appreciate is that as you level up characters learn new skills. As opposed to 7, where skills were tied to weapons. You had to equip a weapon and use its skill enough times to permanently learn it. So you had situations were you were equipping weak weapons just to mash out the skill and learn it. 

	Also, your party now levels up whether they're in battle or not. I'm pretty sure that wasn't in 7. In general, this game is Ys 7 mechanics, but better. The only actual 'negative' in something new is the weapon powering system. It makes no sense. You can spend cash and materials to beef up a sword, but why when the next town has a sword 10x better in the shop? It's only ever useful once you get to end-game weapons.

I love this since the old games had this sense of exploration as well. The only downside is that for as big as the map is it lacks in optional bosses, dungeons, treasures, or quests that make sure of it. It's a map filled with enemies but nothing else. So unless you want a shiny 100% on the map screen it's pointless to explore.

I've played the game on every console it's been released on, and PC is easily the best (Again).

[h1]What I Liked[/h1]
✅ Voice acting (though it's only partial.  Nowhere near as much as Lacrimosa of Dana)

✅ Cutscenes - always love me some cutscenes

✅ The battle engine is simple and easy to get used to.  I also felt the fighting was more frenetic than any other Ys game besides Napishtim; so if you want to really feel "action game", look no further.

✅ The length is just right.  It's not egregiously long and it's not terribly short.  

✅ Decent (not great) character development.

✅ The story is easy to follow and understand especially if you follow the series (nothing is spoiled, just that it does a great job reminding you that Adol's adventure is actually a continuous thread, even though each game is perfectly playable separately.  This makes the Ys series stand out above others - the ability to tell a continual story but still have independently strong games in the series.)

✅ Good music (not the best in the series...that title goes to Lacrimosa of Dana with Napishtim a close second).


[h1]What I Didn't Like[/h1]

⛔ Adol can't jump here...but he can swim.  But in Lacrimosa, he can jump but not swim, in Napishtim he can do (basically) everything, but because Steam didn't get the Konami version, there's no voice acting, thus it's extremely difficult to relate to any of the characters.  Lack of consistency (it's not Celceta's fault, just annoying).  Whereas Monstrum Nox basically throws it all to the wind with wall running and jumping.

⛔ Dogi is shown in a brief cutscene but is otherwise irrelevant to the game.  When you remember that the series was always supposed to be about Adol AND Dogi, it gets frustrating to see Dogi get backseated the way he was here.  

⛔ Some of the plot lines are not fully explored and/or explained poorly.  Remnos, for example.  It's made clear what happened, but not how/why.  Also, secondary antagonists are treated as super powerful only to fall quite easily to Adol and Crew, without any real consequences.

⛔ One way you know an Ys game is the lack of towns...Celceta is the only Ys game so far released that actually did feature multiple (aka more than two) towns (six officially).  That's great, except that it failed to create a compelling reason to revisit said towns outside of questing.  A minor nitpick but I call it out for what it is.

⛔ The "Hug The Map" issue which only applies to this Ys game.  It's infuriating that it was not fixed in the Steam release or even the PS4 remaster (so I'm told).


I still maintain it's a worthy play and one of the more fun games of the era for fans of the genre, but we should delude ourselves into thinking it's perfect.  But based on the demo, it may stand the test of time compared to Monstrum Nox which appears to have regressed (time will tell).

First Impressions:

Ys: Memories of Celceta is a modern remake of Ys IV, which was an ARPG that was originally released on the SNES (in Japan only). Memories of Celceta was originally released on the PS Vita (about 5 years ago) and was subsequently ported to Windows.

I would recommend this game to fans of the series, though those who are unfamiliar with the Ys series may be better advised to check out Ys VIII first: Ys VIII very similar to Memories of Celceta, but with improved graphics, controls and camera. However, I understand that the PC port of YS VIII was terrible on release (I played it on PS4) and Memories of Celceta is less than half the price (£20, compared to a price of £45 for YS VIII), so Memories of Celceta is by no means strictly inferior to YS VIII.
Cool game that's a bit of a slow burn for the first half. Story gets set up for a while but once the game opens up and you have freedom to explore and have fun, the game is peak.

Ys: Memories of Celceta is an action RPG, where you once again take control of a young adventurer named Adol Christin. In the beginning of the game Adol is feeling under the weather - he can barely walk and can't even remember his name. So, the obvious goal is to help Adol regain his memories and find out what happened. Of course, there's more going on behind the scenes, and you can be certain that by the end of the game Adol will have to avert an existential level threat and fight a godlike entity (it wouldn't be a JRPG otherwise).

The game plays like a pretty typical hack and slash affair. You can attack, dodge, block and use offensive skills that consume SP. Even though Adol is the main character you can play as any member of your party, not just him. Plus you can have up to 2 AI controlled party members helping you out on the battlefield. You don't have much control over them other than switching between aggressive and passive behavior (it controls whether they attack enemies). When you're not engaged in combat there's a lot of exploration to be done. The game implements a metroidvania-esque design principle, where certain areas are inaccessible until you acquire a necessary tool, such as Dwarf Bracelet that makes your party members shrink in size and allows them to fit into tiny passages. Similarly, each party member you recruit has a unique skill that can open up new paths or is required to solve puzzles. Speaking of puzzles - there's a fair amount of them in the game. They aren't very challenging, but they aren't insultingly simple either.

Graphically the game looks pretty good, considering its age. However, I'd recommend disabling the HDR effects since they make the game look worse (at least on my non-HDR monitor), drowning everything in bloom. Also, play it in fullscreen (playing it in windowed mode can cause screen tearing and other problems). As for the music - Falcom games have a reputation for having amazing tunes, and this game is no exception.

Overall, Memories of Celceta is a lot of fun to play. A complete playthrough will take about 30 hours, and those would be 30 hours well spent.

Ah [b]Ys: Memories of Celceta[/b], AKA the game where Adol is an amnesiac... Twas a good run, had some flaws but overall a good entry as always.

Idk whether to call this game a remake or a remaster but essentially it's the definitive edition of Ys IV, which had two separate games: [b]Dawn of Ys[/b] and [b]Mask of the Sun[/b]. The story incorporates both of the stories from these two separate titles, making it its own thing and thus, I will judge it as its own entry.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
You play as Adol (the amnesiac) and Co. exploring the uncharted Great Forest of Celceta, rumored to cause those who enter to lose their sense of direction, never to return. The story that will unfold results in the revelation of how Adol attained the moniker "Adventurer", as well as the secrets and upcoming disaster that awaits Adol and his party.

As Adol is an amnesiac this time round, we get the honors of finally seeing just how Adol was like as a kid! Ys I shows part of his childhood but we see how Adol reacts to learning about the world and some of his misadventures as a kid as well.

Gameplay is simple, you fight in a party of 3, with the ability to swap between the current 3 on the fly with the rest in reserve. Having 2 characters with the same damage type will give your party a slight damage boost while having all 3 unique will increase the drop rate of rare items. There are basic attacks (single button combo chain), skills as well as extra skills.

An SP gathering attack can be charged by holding your attack for about a second (charging is shown by the characters glowing, when this glow disappears it means the attack can be unleashed), attacking at this point will charge your SP. When a skill is used, your Extra Gauge will be charged, allowing you to use your [b]Extra Skill[/b] when fully charged.

Evading at the right time executes a [b]Flash Move[/b] which slows down time and renders you invulnerable to all damage while in effect.

[b]Guarding[/b] is an essential part of [b]Memories of Celceta[/b], guarding at the right time gives you [b]Flash Guard[/b], causing all of your attacks to become critical hits for a short period.

Exploration is probably the most open of all the titles (including the newer titles), with lots of optional areas that you can skip, and this shows very well as a rushed playthrough skipping the optional areas could range from about 15-20hours depending on skill while a full 100% playthrough could take over 30 hours. Getting lost is par for the course with this game unless you use a guide. The bulk of the game happens in dungeons outside of exploration.

Bosses involve pattern recognition, learning these and abusing the hell out of [b]Flashes[/b] is integral to beating the game easily.

Each character also have their own special actions that can be executed that are purely situational and help you traverse through the map.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[list]
    [*]30-40 Hours of gameplay from just the main story (up to 50 hours to 100%)
    [*]Uniqute variety of skills that get unique upgrades as you level them
    [*]Very solid gameplay
    [*]Good story, not my favorite from the series but it was still very good
    [*]Unique upgrade system
    [*]The most open map in the series, getting lost is almost guaranteed unless you use a guide, making this game super fun for people who like to explore
    [*]All towns are relevant at all points in the game, with their own facilities and side quests
    [*]Very good port with no issues or bugs that can be gamebreaking
    [*]Young Adol's misadventures are really cute
    [*]I can't decide, Frieda, Karna and Leeza are all too good, so they're all best girls
[/list]

[h1]Things to note if you're coming from any of the newer titles (VIII and IX mainly)[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Flash Guard exists but you don't gain any free invincibility period for it and it lasts much shorter
    [*]No character notes or affinity events
    [*]2 playthroughs are entirely required in order to get 100% completion
    [*]No talismans, everyone has a set damage type
[/list]

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Character skills are too situational, making them feel very useless until you find a spot you have to use it on. Can potentially break the pace entirely just because you have to swap to someone else to proceed before replacing them again because you like playing a different character.
    [*]Swimming SUCKS, [b]Ys VIII[/b] did underwater segments much better. As much as swimming makes sense, the swimming segments are probably the worst parts of the game as you can't use skills and can only use one single attack that takes too long to use to be useful.
    [*]100% requires almost 2 full playthroughs (till the 2nd to last area).
    [*]The fact you can get lost easily may turn some people away
    [*]The upgrade system is a little broken, farming for the materials isn't too hard just tedious so if you're willing to farm for materials, you can make even some of the worst weapons and armors in the game some of the best.
    [*]The fact that you can't access the full strength facilities in a single location makes upgrading and updating gear more annoying than it has to be.
    [*]Port does nothing special, it's just a 1:1 port with no major bugs or glitches.
    [*]THE MAP IS BADLY ALIGNED, YOU HAVE TO HUG THE WALLS IF YOU WANNA 100% THE MAP
[/list]

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
With a good story, open exploration and good gameplay to boot, [b]Memories of Celceta[/b] doesn't fail to live up to what is expected from Ys. Bonus points for the fact that we get to see cute lil' Adol and his childhood! Still a very good game even with its flaws, it's also very cheap so nabbing it at full price is more than well worth it.

[i]I feel like a broken record talking about the Ys franchise lately, but with the recent release of Ys XI: Monstrum Nox by Nippon Ichi Software America (NISA) on all platforms at the time of writing this, I felt compelled to replay the series on Steam. This time, chronologically (not by release date), the next game in line is Memories of Celceta released initially on the PS Vita, then on Steam and recently on the PS4 (definitive edition without mods). I'm sure you will get used to me talking about Ys, though, since there's a few more entries after this one!

Again, the game follows our curious adventurer (and frequent amnesiac), Adol Christin. This time finding himself in the middle of a bustling military town finding that he lost all his memories being the sole known survivor of a mysterious and dangerous forest of Celceta. This journey will see us helping Adol find his memories and explore the treacherous locales of Celceta. [/i]

Sadly, I found Celceta a little wanting on many levels. The characters weren't as lovable as most other games in the franchise, the ending was a very open to interpretation, literally, and the noticeably missing jump mechanic is something I had a hard time accepting. Coming from loving The Ark of Napishtim, the jumping mechanic broke my streak with the franchise.

That being said, my 50 hour journey through Adol's memory searching through uncharted land was still an enjoyable one nonetheless.

[b][i]The story[/i][/b]

Being a JRPG, most story themes are very predictable and tropes have been done before. Celceta borrows those similar tropes. Amnesiac hero who is out to chart the realm and stumbles on a secret that wasn't meant to be discovered. Although, the biggest drawback here is the loose ends once the game (literally) closes the book. What knowledge was Adol supposed to receive? What happened to keeping that area of the land tucked away from the outside world? Where's Dogi (lol)? What happened after the Mask of the Sun was destroyed? Did the world recover (probable yes)? Did Eldeel end up retiring? The Akashik Records were...destroyed? At the end of the day, the big take away was Adol's official god-given title of "Adventurer"? No long term friendships or memorabilia? So many questions at the end, really. Although, small plot lines like Griselda's actual rank and stake in the Romun Empire were described through smaller side quests, most are left open ended.

[b][i]The action[/i][/b]

Ys Seven was the first entry that got rid of jumping and instated a party mechanic. I'm not a total fan of either, really, but I acknowledge the party feature more than the lack of jumping (which, spoilers to this series of reviews, comes back in Lacrimosa of Dana and beyond!). Ys I and II did not have a jump mechanic, but it was understandable given the limitations and the combat mechanics of the game. In terms of release date, though, the era of Napishtim (2003), Felghana (2005) and Origin (2006) were one of the cleanest combat mechanics in the franchise in terms of being simple and solid all-around. I really liked that depending on the progress of Adol's jump the attack would differ from a rising spin to a downward slam. These small things make so much difference.

Obviously, I'm very upset with the removal of jumping. LOL

Otherwise, Celceta has a robust combat system albeit a little button-mashy. This drastically changes once you up the difficulty, though. Combat can be very tight. The SP system for active skills that can be leveled up to get stronger is a very dynamic one. The ultimate skills per character are really flashy and come around when needed. And the party mechanic is decent in terms of mixing things up a little through a very long journey. Each party member will represent an attack type that will work better or worse against certain enemy types, which (unfortunately) stops you from making favorites in the game.

[b][i]The Overall Package[/i][/b]

Similar to a lot of JRPGs, the last stage is drawn out. I was seething to finally finish the game when I realize that the very final part of the game's last stage was split into sections and the epilogue was drawn out. Sometimes, when I'm nearing the end of the story, I just want it to hit like a bus and be done with it. Instead, we get a long bus ride to get to somewhere we already knew we were heading towards. Not a deal breaker, but definitely something to take with me in my studies: don't prolong the end!

Being such a fan of the Ys series since my discovery of the series on the PSP with The Ark of Napishtim, I have to say that despite the setting of Memories of Celceta, it is definitely one of the weaker games in the franchise for me. That being said, some features in Celceta and Seven have evolved for the better in the later games. Progress!

...So much for doing the franchise chronologically like I initially said up above, but I'm digging into Lacrimosa of Dana before hitting Oath in Felghana again since my original playthroughs on handheld.

That being said, my biggest gripe with the game was not being able to get all the sun stones in one run, which I fixed for my save as I felt as though I had gotten everything I wanted from the game by 100%ing everything else in the run. But that is me being more nit-picky than anything else. Again, highly recommend giving this game a shot!

Short take: 8.5/10, weaker of the Ys games with obtuse early puzzles and a slow starter of a plot, but still strong for the genre.

Long take:
Admittedly, it's one of the weaker of the Ys games, but that still places it above most other Action RPGs overall. I'm a long time fan, having played every game except IX and the original IV's, but this one is a slow starter. When it does get going, it gets pretty annoying at first with the first split path.

Now, I like the idea of player choice in principle. The problem is that not only do both of these paths involve the irritating and lazy Lost Woods trope, but one of them is clearly the one you're supposed to go to first as the other has higher level mobs. For some reason, nobody thought to implement level scaling, and so doing them out of "order" results in the first being brutally difficult and the second being a cakewalk. The second split path has this issue as well, but the level differences (~41 versus ~44) don't really impact gameplay much by then.

To make matters worse, I had stopped playing around this part of the game due to not having enough free time. I did so at one of the most obtuse parts of the game -- the water dungeon where there's a specific angle you must go beneath a current to be able to progress. I was flat out stuck until others on GameFAQs also called BS on that section and explained how to get past.

Though in spite of these early flaws, it gets better. The balance improves, the puzzles are less obtuse, and the story really gets going. It's a shame it doesn't hit the ground running like other Ys titles, but when it does, it's a fantastic game.

Anyway, here's some obligatory section scoring:

Gameplay: 7/10, obtuse puzzles early on brought this down.
Controls: 10/10, every Ys game (and remake) starting with VI controls like an extension of yourself, if you had superpowers.
Story: 8.5/10, likable, somewhat bog standard, gets monotonous with the first 3 villages.
Sound: 10/10, I mean it's Ys. Action RPG with great soundtrack is a given. Partially voiced is fine, as I can read. :P
Graphics: 8/10, good stylized graphics, some conspicuous low res textures with important backgrounds though. (like the diamond puzzle)
Overall: 8.5/10, weak for Ys but still worth your money if you like Action RPGs.

So, this game leaves me with mixed feelings. I had played almost no JRPGs until a year ago, and have been slowly making my way through classic series. From a gameplay perspective, so far the Ys series has blown everything out of the water. Final Fantasy and the like have good narratives, but Ys has gameplay that challenges you, and makes you enjoy conquering challenges. I honestly don't understand why people got, so excited about Dark Souls, given that apparently a tradition of challenge has existed since the late 80's in Japan.

So far I have played Ys I&II and Ys: Origin and both games were better than Celceta, but this is only a testament to the quality of the series so far. Memories of Celceta is easily a game worth playing. Decent story, lovely characters, good soundtrack, and fun gameplay are strong enough arguments to justify the full price of the game.

In depth review:

Positives:

+ Graphics - given that this is a PS Vita port, the graphics are actually shockingly good. The art style makes the lack of detail unnoticeable, and the visual effects and lighting contribute to a great atmosphere. There is a distinct visual style to each set of areas and you can feel the atmosphere wherever you are -  whether a sunny cliff or mysterious dark cave. The enemy design, especially bosses is original and non-repetitive. Evolved variants of basic enemies look tougher, instead of just being recolored. It is clear that a lot has gone into making the game look great both in its initial release and on this platform as well.

+ Story - although not as gripping as some of the previous stories, the mystery of Celceta keeps you interested, and the colorful characters provide story beats that are amusing and even at times stimulating. Maybe the impact would have been even greater if the pace of the story was not broken up with the huge sections of gameplay in between, but it's still good enough to justify at least one playthrough. It would have been nice if my second Nightmare playthrough on Nightmare would have netted a couple of extra shots here and there :*(.

+ Music - like the previous enemies listed the music is above industry average. There are a couple of truly great tracks, but the rest are just decent. With the other Ys games I've played so far, the bar was set so high when it came to music that maybe I am unfairly judging the level here, but it left me a bit disappointed. Still, it surpasses the average for a AAA game, and the couple of tracks previously mentioned will make their way onto my playlists.

Mixed:

= Gameplay - Celceta's gameplay is great on one hand - duh, Ys game. It's fast and kinetic, the way I like games to play. I left the game idling, so my game time is inflated, but I still spent roughly 70 hours on it. Feeling each blow of a combo is a big deal for me (216 hrs in Arkham City, so far), and even though Ys games have simple combat mechanics, skillful use makes watching experienced players and attaining mastery yourself a pleasure.

    Celceta, however, suffers from a problem. Instead of making you learn enemy attack patterns and effective patterns to kill them, this Ys game relies on the use of Flash Guard and Flash Move. Now, I began playing the game on Nightmare because I didn't know that a 2nd playthrough was obligatory for 100% completion, and I typically try to play the most challenging difficulty and get everything done in one go. Still, if the game is as awesome to play as Ys Origin, I don't mind going through it multiple times. However, Nightmare in Celceta meant that the first boss was a bit challenging until I found out how exactly Flash Guard and Flash Move can be used, and then I proceeded to mush everything int the game apart from the Super Boss in one or two tries, and I would have gotten him as well if hadn't tried to take him on at level 52 for the first time.

    Ys bosses are typically awesome, each one forcing you to move differently and explore their weaknesses. Ys I & II are especially amazing in that regard. Almost every boss in the previous three games I played required you to apply an amazing amount of skilled effort to beat on the highest difficulty, and luck had little to do with whether you emerged victorious (except for Dark Fact - he will be remembered in the nightmares of all who faced him on the highest difficulty). Here, I would learn the attack patterns and then proceed to just Guard and Dodge and beat almost every boss in the exact same way. Now, there were ones that had weird attacks where they raided you, or tried to go for heals, but it was still Dash Attack to get SP, Flash Guard Counter, hit with skill, repeat and drop in Extra Skill whenever you can.

     Also, the challenge in Nightmare is provided mostly by the health pool of the enemy. I fought the fish boss with him landing one or two blows until I learned his pattern and then basically me just running around for 20+ minutes. And apparently it wasn't due to underleveling because it was the same in Time Attack where the level and weapons of characters are fixed. Fights in Origin felt way more challenging, at least to me because the intensity of the boss attacks (*cough* Kishgal *cough*) was such that even though the battle was over in minutes, you still felt satisfied with your achievement.

     Overall, the gameplay is fun, but not on the level of the first three games.

I played this after going through a good chunk of the series (Ys I & II, Napishtim, Felghana, Origin, Seven), and I have to say: this one definitely leans more into RPG territory, while still keeping that sweet Ys combat I love.

Compared to the usual ~15h entries, this one is a bit of a chonker. If you’re looking for a quick weekend rush through monsters and music, maybe pick another title. If you're okay with a longer adventure, strap in.

Difficulty:
I usually play Ys games on Normal and find the challenge pretty balanced — bosses generally put up a good fight (except Felghana, which is a gym membership disguised as a game).
In Celceta, though? It’s a cakewalk. On Normal, bosses fold faster than cheap lawn chairs. Might be worth bumping the difficulty up if you want any real resistance.

Pros:
Combat is as fast and flashy as ever. There’s a solid variety of skills, and leveling them up sometimes gives a fun little twist — like a bonus AoE or an extra hit. It's like surprise seasoning in your attack soup.

More RPG systems than usual: crafting, gathering, upgrading gear… basically, it’s Adol with a to-do list.

Exploration is fun and rewarding. Uncovering the map is surprisingly satisfying. Bonus points if you're a map completionist who can't rest until every pixel is revealed.

Visually, it’s a nice step up from Seven. I wasn’t a big fan of Seven’s "early PS2 vibes", but Celceta looks and feels more polished.

The soundtrack slaps, as is tradition. Falcom never misses here.

Cons:
The story isn’t bad, but it’s kind of like the salad before the main course — you eat it, it’s fine, but you’re really here for the meat (aka gameplay).

Some dungeons felt a bit short and less complex than in earlier games. I wouldn't have minded getting lost a few more times.

The underwater combat? Yeah… we don't talk about that. Let’s just say fish aren’t meant to be fought with swords, and leave it at that.

Final thoughts:
If you like Ys games, you’ll have fun here. It’s not the peak of the series (so far for me), but it’s a solid entry with great combat, music, and exploration. Just maybe crank the difficulty up a notch — unless you're here to watch Adol speedrun his way through boss fights while barely blinking.
